messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting latent class models in two-way contingency table
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Fitting latent class models in two-way contingency table
messages.body_plain:
It's helpful for us to help diagnose your problem if you
cut and paste the exact message you're getting into your
mail.  Otherwise, we have to guess what the "some problem" is.

Your model has a number of bugs.

1.  alpha1, alpha2, beta1, and beta2 all need to be declared
as simplexes because they're variants drawn from Dirichlet priors.
Daniel noticed they had to be vectors, but the requirement's
even stricter than that.  In Stan, the constraints on the variables
need to match the support.

So that's

  simplex[3] alpha1;
  ...

2.  I have no idea what you want to do with this:

culm ~ multinomial(theta[1] * alpha1[j] * beta1[k]
                   + theta[2] * alpha2[j] * beta2[k]);

but the argument to multinomial() needs to be a 9-simplex (a
size 9 vector with non-negative entries summing to 1).
As is, you get a single scalar, because all those indexed
variables are simplexes.

I also don't understand why it's a doubly-nested loop.  You
wind up sampling the same data, culm, 9 times.

If you're trying to create some kind of mixture model, there's a chapter in
the manual on how to do that.

Rather than using a 2-simplex, it's easier to understand and more efficient
to just use a single variable constrained to <lower=0,upper=1>.  Then you
can put a beta prior on it instead of a Dirichlet and get exactly the
same posterior for theta with:

parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
  ...
model {
  theta ~ beta(a[1],a[2]);
  ...
      culm ~ multinomial(theta*alpha1[j]*beta1[k] + (1 - theta)*alpha2[j]*beta2[k]);

The right side of this still won't compile because it's just a scalar
and you need a simplex.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to both of you.  I hadn't thought about relative
error being unstable with values near 0.

And I can see how you'd need to tune if you had diff eqs
on radically different scales, because if your variables scale
is 1e9, then I'm not likely to get 1e-6 absolute error tolerances,
whereas if the variable scale is 1e-9, then 1e-6 is too large.
out.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] MStan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] MStan?
messages.body_plain:
Awesome --- this looks great.  Thanks for letting
everyone know.

Would you mind if we linked that from our top-level
web site, mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>?  I'd create a page mirroring this
one and include a navbar:

  http://mc-stan.org/pystan.html

Presumably I should call it "MatlabStan" instead of
"MStan"?

Thanks for including clear licensing terms (BSD, to boot).
And some full working examples.

I also take it this is Matlab-only and won't work in Octave?
I'm not a user of either one, I just want to know how to describe
it on the web page.

You're also welcome to move the repo to stan-dev if you'd
prefer.  Otherwise, I can just create links to your repo.

- Bob

> I updated the process-level Matlab wrapper for Stan
>   * exposes some new parameters from Stan 2.4.0 (optimization)
>   * changes so that it runs on Windows
>   * function for calculating WAIC (based on R code from Vehtari & Gelman)
>
> More details here:
>
> https://github.com/brian-lau/MatlabStan/wiki
>
> -b

> On Saturday, January 11, 2014 1:21:34 PM UTC+1, Brian Lau wrote:
> I've got a process-level wrapper here:
>
> https://github.com/brian-lau/MatlabStan
>
> I'll get some better docs up in the next week, although some effort went into following Pystan/Rstan conventions, so some of those docs could be useful.
>
> Joachim, maybe it's worth merging?
>
> -b
>
> On Friday, January 10, 2014 11:20:01 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 1/10/14, 9:54 AM, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Do you have any useful estimate when MStan (Matlab/Octave interface) might be available?
>
> When we find a volunteer who knows MATLAB and wants to do it :-)
>
> > Or how should I proceed if I would like to help implement that?
>
> There are two ways to create an interface.
>
> 1.  Process-level wrapper
> Just write code in MATLAB to dump the data in a format we can read,
> call Stan in a separate process(es) to write samples out, then write
> code to read back in the results into MATLAB and ideally do some posterior
> analysis.
>
> 2.  In-memory wrapper
> This is what we've done for PyStan and RStan.  It's a lot more work,
> but potentially much faster and definitely more flexible (e.g., it
> makes it easy to expose the log prob functions and gradients/Hessians.
> MATLAB has a package (whose name I forget) that makes that possible.
>
> One of the things we're going to try to do over the next 12 months
> is clean up the underlying C++ code to make approach (2) easier
> and more consistent across our interfaces.  Right now, everything
> that's in stan/gm/command.hpp needs to be reimplemented in each
> interface.
>
> - Bob
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Metropolis rejection aren't a problem as long as they occur only early during initialization / warmup when Stan is still adjusting the stepsize of the sampling algorithm (stepping outside the support of parameters leads to a Metropolis rejection). If you get these messages (it's not an error) during sampling, your model may be ill-conditioned and you need to find out what's causing it.

Just to check: did you intend to use gamma priors for the standard deviations. The way you parameterized them (ultra-vague prior) is reminiscent of inverse-gamma distribution as conjugate prior for variance. However, these priors usually have to much mass close to zero (which I guess is why you truncated them). In BUGS, the normal distribution is specified in terms of mean and precision; in Stan, it's mean and standard deviation, so in your model the prior is not conjugate. You might just as well use a half-Cauchy prior for standard deviation (no truncation needed as long as the support in the parameters block is lower=0 and the hyperparameters of the prior are fixed).

The truncation in your code leads to another thing: you don't need to do it if it you've defined the support of the parameter AND the parameters feeding into the desired truncated distribution are fixed. Truncation will add something to the log-posterior, and if the parameters of the truncated distribution are fixed, the addition will be constant (so totally unnecessary). I.e. you can drop the truncations in the priors for standard deviations.

That hybrid can be used for a complete data likelihood and you should also model the probability that an observation is NA, presumably as a function of the hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector. However, this is all moot if you have missingness on discrete valued data because Stan does not permit you to declare discrete unknowns in the parameter block. Maybe just maybe you can do some data augmentation thing where you have continuous unknowns underlying discrete observables, but that is going to be tedious at best.
> > > >
> > > > Basically, Stan sucks at the sort of missing data problems that are commonplace in practice and this is the one area where the BUGS family of software has the biggest advantage over Stan. Although such models tend to be slow at best with BUGS and have at least as many problems with convergence, mixing, etc. as models for fully observed data.

Am Mittwoch, 1. Oktober 2014 12:55:52 UTC+2 schrieb Luc Coffeng:
> Metropolis rejection aren't a problem as long as they occur only early during initialization / warmup when Stan is still adjusting the stepsize of the sampling algorithm (stepping outside the support of parameters leads to a Metropolis rejection). If you get these messages (it's not an error) during sampling, your model may be ill-conditioned and you need to find out what's causing it.
>
> Just to check: did you intend to use gamma priors for the standard deviations. The way you parameterized them (ultra-vague prior) is reminiscent of inverse-gamma distribution as conjugate prior for variance. However, these priors usually have to much mass close to zero (which I guess is why you truncated them). In BUGS, the normal distribution is specified in terms of mean and precision; in Stan, it's mean and standard deviation, so in your model the prior is not conjugate. You might just as well use a half-Cauchy prior for standard deviation (no truncation needed as long as the support in the parameters block is lower=0 and the hyperparameters of the prior are fixed).
>
> The truncation in your code leads to another thing: you don't need to do it if it you've defined the support of the parameter AND the parameters feeding into the desired truncated distribution are fixed. Truncation will add something to the log-posterior, and if the parameters of the truncated distribution are fixed, the addition will be constant (so totally unnecessary). I.e. you can drop the truncations in the priors for standard deviations.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

Apologies in advance for my question, which is really more of a clarification.

I have a model written for jags that runs well but slowly. I want to use the model on a large (150,000+ cases) dataset and it will probably take too long with jags.

My question is, is there anything obvious in the model below that would not translate to stan?

---
model{

for(i in 1:N){

  w[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
  logit(p[i]) <- a0 + (b0 * x1[i])
  test[i] <- step(w[i] - 1) + 1

}

for(i in 1:N){

  y[i] ~ dnorm(y.hat[i], tau[test[i]])
  y.hat[i] <- a1[test[i]] + (b1[test[i]] * x2[i])

}

a0 ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
b0 ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
a1[2] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
a1[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
b1[2] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
b1[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
tau[1] <- pow(sigma[1], -2)
sigma[1] ~ dunif(0, 100)
tau[2] <- pow(sigma[2], -2)
sigma[2] ~ dunif(0, 100)

}
---

Specifically, the jags model is designed to allow for:
missing values in the response variable w; all other variables are complete
a step function or ifelse statement to switch between different coefficients in the linear regression
interactions among categorical variables, with the possibility to set a contrast as 0

Are all these features available in stan? My reading suggests that they are but I need to be sure before attempting to rewrite my code.

Thanks in advance for any insight,

Stephen

Hm tricky one as I'm not familiar with the model itself. Some further observations:

you can drop the truncation on the statements like temp1_mu ~ normal(2.5624,2.0327)T[0,] as the parameters are fixed, so the truncation only adds a constant to the log-posterior. Statements like k1[i] ~ normal(k1_mu,k1_lambda)T[0,] do need the truncation as the parameters aren't fixed, so truncation adds a non-constant number to the log-posterior, which is important for the gradient.
ah, the cause of your Metropolis rejections is that you have defined the support for k1_mu and k3_mu to be <lower=0>, whereas the priors do not cover only part of the positive real numbers. So what happens is that on the unconstrained scale, the sampler samples a number, exponentiates it to satisfy the support <lower=0> (and adds the Jacobian of the transformation to the posterior to correct the curvature), and then sometimes finds that the density doesn't exist because you tell the model that the density does not exist outside the range of the priors in the model block. Fix: match the support in the parameter block with the domain that your prior in your model block covers. Once you've done this, you can even leave out the prior from the model block if it's uniform, as this is the standard in Stan (i.e. if you specify the support in the parameter block to be <lower=-1,upper=1>, you effectively say that the parameter has a uniform distribution between -1 and 1, unless you specify a prior in the model block that says otherwise. The manual should provide insight into the mechanics behind this).

messages.body_plain:
It helps to know what's data and what's parameters to figure out
how a JAGS model translates to Stan.

Stan doesn't have integer parameters, so you can't implement missing
w directly.

There is an if_else() in Stan, but also full conditional statements,
which are usually easier to read.  And local variables.  If you see
step() being used in a Stan model, it's usually just a straight translation
from BUGS/JAGS that can be improved.

Stan gives you a logit-scaled Bernoulli.  So rather than writing

  for (i in 1:N)
    y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(theta[i]));

you can write

  for (i in 1:N)
    y[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(theta[i]);

and then once you've done that you can vectorize to

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

Unless you expect parameters on the scale of 100, use tighter
priors than precision=1e-3 (sd=100).  For comparison, Stan's
normal uses the standard deviation/scale parameterization, not
precision or variance (both precision and covariance matrices
available for multinormals).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
For missing w it depends what you want to do with it.

If you just need to impute values, you can generate those in
the generated_quantities block, though it's more efficient
statistically to work in terms of expectations.  It works like
this on the logit scale:

   w_missing[i] <- bernoulli_logit_rng(...);

You'll also want to define test in the generated quantities block
as nothing depends on it in the model.  It's more efficient and
clearer in terms of intent that way.  The generated quantities block is
where predictive quantities go that don't impact estimation.

If you want the missing w to impact estimation, then you need to
marginalize out the w explicitly in the model.  You basically get
a mixture model over the two outcomes, w[i] = 0 and w[i] = 1.  There's
a chapter in the manual, and a whole new chapter with more examples coming
in Stan 2.5 (out real soon, as in hopefully the next month).

That is, where you currently have

  PROD_i bernoulli(w[i] | inv_logit(a0 + b0 * x1[i]))

you need to marginalize out the w.  But I don't see any reason you'd
want to do that as it won't impact the estimates in the model you have
because the two blocks in your model are completely separated and w doesn't
appear anywhere else.

- Bob

> It's helpful for us to help diagnose your problem if you

> mail.  Otherwise, we have to guess what the "some problem" is.
>
> Your model has a number of bugs.
>
> 1.  alpha1, alpha2, beta1, and beta2 all need to be declared
> as simplexes because they're variants drawn from Dirichlet priors.
> Daniel noticed they had to be vectors, but the requirement's
> even stricter than that.  In Stan, the constraints on the variables
> need to match the support.
>
> So that's
>
>   simplex[3] alpha1;
>   ...
>
> 2.  I have no idea what you want to do with this:
>
> culm ~ multinomial(theta[1] * alpha1[j] * beta1[k]
>                    + theta[2] * alpha2[j] * beta2[k]);
>
> but the argument to multinomial() needs to be a 9-simplex (a
> size 9 vector with non-negative entries summing to 1).
> As is, you get a single scalar, because all those indexed
> variables are simplexes.
>
> I also don't understand why it's a doubly-nested loop.  You
> wind up sampling the same data, culm, 9 times.
>
> If you're trying to create some kind of mixture model, there's a chapter in
> the manual on how to do that.
>
> Rather than using a 2-simplex, it's easier to understand and more efficient
> to just use a single variable constrained to <lower=0,upper=1>.  Then you
> can put a beta prior on it instead of a Dirichlet and get exactly the
> same posterior for theta with:
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
>   ...

>   theta ~ beta(a[1],a[2]);
>   ...

messages.body_plain:
There are errors in both your arguments.  The error message is
saying you have two real arguments, but what multinomial expects
is an integer array outcome of counts and a vector parameter
whose content is a simplex (non-negative entries summing to 1).

As I said last time, what you wrote down,

  theta[1] * alpha1[j] * beta1[k] + theta[2] * alpha2[j] * beta2[k],

is a scalar.  And if you have a single outcome, you want categorical(),
not multinomial(), and that outcome needs to be an integer.

Check out the description of multinomial in the manual.  I'm afraid
we don't have time to do a tutorial one e-mail post at a time.

If you have a working BUGS or JAGS implementation of the model, that
might help isolate your programming errors.

- Bob

messages.subject: negative binomial confusing doc
messages.subject_clean: negative binomial confusing doc
messages.body_plain:
I don't have posting privileges to stan-devel, so I'll post here (I emailed too, overkill is good :) ).

What makes negative binomial parametrization complicated includes the scale vs. rate parametrization choice for the gamma, and the question is the negative binomial the distribution of k failures before r successes (r is fixed, k starts at 0), or how many trials are needed before r failures (r is fixed, k starts at r), or a Poisson/Gamma mixture. It's all, of course, but that changes the meaning of some of the parameters.

In the first (Gelman) version, Gelman uses the rate parametrization of the Gamma, but calls it "inverse scale" instead of rate (which is correct, rate = 1/scale), so calling it "inverse scale" in the NBinom is consistent (as is done in Appendix A of BDA3).

The second version is an alternative parametrization of the Negative binomial based on its variance to mean (which is 1 + inverse scale) but the V2M is not one of the explicit parameters. Doing it this way makes the NB depend explicitly on the mean as one of its parameters. Running through the algebra, mu, being the mean, is equivalent to Version 1's alpha / beta and so phi must be equal to alpha. To be consistent, I would call phi there the shape as per version 1, and call mu either the mean or location. Phi isn't the inverse scale any more than alpha is--they are identical.

R itself refers to alpha/r/phi as the "size" as well as "shape" (due to its being the gamma's shape).

Of course, to my continued frustration, the parametrization I use for the negative binomial is the one where beta is the scale itself, not the rate or V2M (as per DeGroot or Klugman, Panjer, Wilmot), so I'm used to seeing :

NB = Choose(r + k -1, k) * (b / (1+b)) ^ k * (1 / (1+b)) ^ r

Where r = alpha = phi and my_beta = 1 / your_beta = mu / phi.

Which makes for a loglikihood of:

lnΓ(r + k) - lnΓ(r) - lnΓ(k + 1) + k * ln(b) - (r + k) * ln(1 + b)

which I think is simpler than the other two. I'd request that be added too, but I understand if you feel having three negative binomial parametrizations in Stan and its documentation is a harbinger for the zombie apocalypse.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks --- that was really helpful.

I think we'll eventually add more negative binomials.
The parameterizations really make a difference for MCMC,
both for HMC samplers like Stan and for Gibbs samplers like
JAGS.

I think having multiple parameterizations is good in that it
simplifies the models and helps prevent coding errors.   I just
want consistent doc so the errors don't get introduced in
interpreting the functions.

I think what would be nice is a big table of how to
inter-translate parameters in all the different parameterizations.

I'd also like

I think we may eventually move to some even more Stan-friendly
parameterizations, like a normal parameterized with log standard deviation,
for example.  It would make it easy to use a lognormal prior and also
saves a transform plus Jacobian and trades a log for an exp in the
density computation.

And some parameterizations that are better suited to hierarchial priors,
like a beta and dirichlet on the mean/total count scale.

Anyone have any suggestions on naming conventions?  I'm unhappy
with neg_binomial2, but it seemed better than just passing
on suffixes indefinitely, like neg_binomial_shape_inverse_scale.
We've used the scale elsewhere, as in poisson_log() and multi_normal_cholesky().

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There are two ways I can see to do this.

My preferred suggestion would be to alpha to start at t+1,
replacing

> for (j in 1:J) {
> >             alpha[j,1] ~ normal(recentered_alpha1[j], 0.001);
> >             sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0,0.25);
> >             for (t in 2:T)
> >                 alpha[j,t] ~ normal(alpha[j,t-1], sigma_alpha);
> > }

with

parameters {
  matrix[J,T-1] alpha;
...
model {
  sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0,0.25);  // this should go on outside, not be repeated

  for (j in 1:J)

    alpha[j,1] ~ normal(recentered_alpha[j], sigma_alpha);

  for (t in 2:T)

    for (j in 1:J)

      alpha[j,t] ~ normal(alpha[j,t-1], sigma_alpha);

...

Then, I'd suggest transposing alpha in the parameterization and
writing the above in vector form as:

  alpha[j] ~ normal(recentered_alpha, sigma_alpha);

  for (t in 2:T)

    alpha[t] ~ normal(alpha[t-1], sigma_alpha);

It'd be most efficient if alpha were declared as an array of vectors:

parameters {
  vector[J] alpha[T-1];

If you really don't want to do that, you can use the col() extractor
to pull columns out.

If you really want to keep alpha all together (I'm not looking through the
rest of your model), then you can do roughly the same thing, change the
names a bit, and then paste alpha back together in the transformed paramters
block.

parameters {

  matrix[J,T-1] alpha_raw;
  ...
transformed parameters {
  matrix[J,T] alpha;

  for (j in 1:J)

    alpha[j,1] <- recentered_alpha[j];

    for (t in 2:T)

      alpha[j,t] <- alpha[j,t-1];
}

It'll create a lot of redundant output if you save alpha_raw (only
option in CmdStan, but you can delete variables on the fly in RStan
and presumably in PyStan).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Can I raise a square matrix to a power? Not elementwise, but where the result of Q^n is is Q matrix-multiplied by itself n-1 times. I understand that pow() doesn't do this. I could use eigenvectors * eigenvalues^n * eigenvectors^-1, but eigenvalues_sym and eigenvectors_sym require a symmetric matrix and Q is not symmetric.

Thanks for any help,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for your explanation. Are you referring to chapter 9 on Mixture Modeling in the Stan 2.4.0 manual?

Actually, I want estimation of w to impact the estimation of y: I want uncertainty in w estimation (particularly missing w) to propagate to uncertainty in y estimation. I'm not convinced I achieve this in the bugs model I shared, which returns very similar estimates to the "combined block" model below.

I'm want to apply this model to animal length data where w is a variable indicating whether the animal is a young of the year (w == 0) or not (w == 1) and y is animal length as a function of several possible environmental drivers.

I have two questions:
    - age is usually determined by length and so length is a predictor of age (w): is this OK? Perhaps there is circularity here that complicates estimation?
    - if the above is OK, then is mixture modeling using Stan (or MCMC generally) a suitable approach to this problem?

Thanks again for your help,
Stephen

## "combined block" model that returns very similar estimates to a model separating the dbern and dnorm estimations:

model{
  for(i in 1:N){

    Age[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
    logit(p[i]) <- a0 + b0[River[i]] + (c0 * Lgth[i])

    test[i] <- step(Age[i] - 1) + 1

#   }
#
#   for(i in 1:N){

    Length[i] ~ dnorm(y.hat[i], tau[test[i]])
    y.hat[i] <- a1[test[i]] + b1[test[i], River[i]]

  }

  a0 ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
  b0[1] <- 0
  c0 ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
  b1[1, 1] <- 0
  b1[2, 1] <- 0
  for(r in 2:N.rivers){
    b0[r] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
    b1[1, r] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
    b1[2, r] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)

  }
  a1[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)
  a1[2] ~ dnorm(0, 1e-3)

  tau[1] <- pow(sigma[1], -2)
  sigma[1] ~ dunif(0, 100)
  tau[2] <- pow(sigma[2], -2)
  sigma[2] ~ dunif(0, 100)

}

On Wednesday, October 1, 2014 6:39:11 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> For missing w it depends what you want to do with it.
>
> If you just need to impute values, you can generate those in
> the generated_quantities block, though it's more efficient
> statistically to work in terms of expectations.  It works like
> this on the logit scale:
>
>    w_missing[i] <- bernoulli_logit_rng(...);
>
> You'll also want to define test in the generated quantities block
> as nothing depends on it in the model.  It's more efficient and
> clearer in terms of intent that way.  The generated quantities block is
> where predictive quantities go that don't impact estimation.
>
> If you want the missing w to impact estimation, then you need to
> marginalize out the w explicitly in the model.  You basically get
> a mixture model over the two outcomes, w[i] = 0 and w[i] = 1.  There's
> a chapter in the manual, and a whole new chapter with more examples coming
> in Stan 2.5 (out real soon, as in hopefully the next month).
>
> That is, where you currently have
>
>   PROD_i bernoulli(w[i] | inv_logit(a0 + b0 * x1[i]))
>
> you need to marginalize out the w.  But I don't see any reason you'd
> want to do that as it won't impact the estimates in the model you have
> because the two blocks in your model are completely separated and w doesn't
> appear anywhere else.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Oct 1, 2014, at 1:25 PM, Stephen <stephenda...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi Bob,

> > Thanks for your quick response. I attach the R code to run the model in jags.

> > The data in the model are: w, x1 and x2.

> > RE missing w: how might I go about accounting for missing w?

> > Thanks for all the other tips.
> >
> > All the best,
> > Stephen
> >
> > On Wednesday, October 1, 2014 6:02:52 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > It helps to know what's data and what's parameters to figure out
> > how a JAGS model translates to Stan.
> >
> > Stan doesn't have integer parameters, so you can't implement missing
> > w directly.
> >
> > There is an if_else() in Stan, but also full conditional statements,
> > which are usually easier to read.  And local variables.  If you see
> > step() being used in a Stan model, it's usually just a straight translation
> > from BUGS/JAGS that can be improved.
> >
> > Stan gives you a logit-scaled Bernoulli.  So rather than writing
> >
> >   for (i in 1:N)
> >     y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(theta[i]));
> >
> > you can write
> >
> >   for (i in 1:N)
> >     y[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(theta[i]);
> >
> > and then once you've done that you can vectorize to
> >
> >   y ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);
> >
> > Unless you expect parameters on the scale of 100, use tighter
> > priors than precision=1e-3 (sd=100).  For comparison, Stan's
> > normal uses the standard deviation/scale parameterization, not
> > precision or variance (both precision and covariance matrices
> > available for multinormals).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > On Oct 1, 2014, at 12:25 PM, Stephen <stephenda...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Dear Stan users,
> > >
> > > Apologies in advance for my question, which is really more of a clarification.
> > >
> > > I have a model written for jags that runs well but slowly. I want to use the model on a large (150,000+ cases) dataset and it will probably take too long with jags.
> > >
> > > My question is, is there anything obvious in the model below that would not translate to stan?
> > >
> > > ---
> > > model{
> > >
> > > for(i in 1:N){
> > >
> > >   w[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
> > >   logit(p[i]) <- a0 + (b0 * x1[i])
> > >   test[i] <- step(w[i] - 1) + 1

> > >
> > > }
> > >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Are these jags model features possible in stan
messages.body_plain:
Yes, that's a mixture model where w is the "indicator" variable
for the mixture.  In Stan, w will have to be marginalized out
of the log probability.  You will be able to recover the posterior
expectation of w for each animal, but you won't get samples.

I'm attaching the new manual chapter, which should provide some
more examples.  It'll be out in Stan 2.5 and all of the models
in it should work in 2.4 as is.

Rather than

  step(Age[i] - 1)

you can write

   (Age[i] > 1)

in Stan.

As to the first question, you will indeed run into problems if you try
to do this:

  u ~ regression based on v
  v ~ regression based on u

To get that effect, you need to formulate a consistent joint model of (u,v).
The usual approach here, if I understand what you're trying to do, is
to just draw the mixture component from a Bernoulli and then based on its
outcome do a regression based on it as you did below.  You don't want to also
do a regression for w based on the length.  The effect of the length on the
choice of w still comes in indirectly because the nodes are connected in
the graphical model, so they're not independent in the posterior.

- Bob

This message doesn't indicate a bug.  Is there something
specific you think is wrong?

We're getting rid of word "Error" in the next release and
hoping that cuts down on the confusion we've created among
our users with this message.

> A separate question that I would like to confirm with you. Would a simple switch from the first line below to the second give me the exact lp__ samples that I can use to calculate the WAIC?
> y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[n] * beta, c);

> increment_log_probit(ordered_logistic_log(x[n] * beta, c));

Yes, if you replace all of the ~ with increment_log_prob (not "increment_log_probit")
then you'll get the full log probability function with no dropped terms.

>
> Here are things wrong with that model at a glance:
>
> 1.  Stan has a built-in ordered logit distribution and you really want
> to be using that.
>
> 2.  If you have a variable with constrained support, as in T[1,100] in

>
> 3.  If you have truncations and have the support defined properly, then
> you never need to have a T[...] truncation with just constants.
>
> 4.  Rather than doing transpose(row(P,i)), which involves lots of extra
> copying, it's better to set up the data structure for P so that it is
> an array of vectors.  See the manual chapter (near the beginning) on
> arrays vs. vectors.
>
> Mitzi's taking a pass through the ARM models, and will probably get
> around to fixing this one.  Peter might have time to fix it before then.
>

On a related note I was wondering if Stan is aware of the generative nature of some models. John.

On Oct 7, 2014, at 2:28 PM, John Reid <johnba...@gmail.com> wrote:

...

> On a related note I was wondering if Stan is aware of the generative nature of some models. Most models I work with are described in terms of conditional distributions that have a natural order from hyperparameters through latent variables to data. I have had success initialising Stan using draws from the prior when the default "random" method didn't do so well. Are there any plans to incorporate some sort of initialisation like this? This would save users recoding their priors in init() functions (which can be error-prone).

Short answers: No and no.

This has been something Andrew's been asking for, too.
But as is, Stan has no knowledge of any generative structure
in the model, so until we add a layer on top to deal with
directed graphical models or some more restricted class, we
don't have any hooks on which to hang such an implementation.

But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
work, Stan would also be able to just converge.

Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
makes a big difference?  If so, we'd love to collect them as
test cases.

My understanding is that JAGS just initializes from the prior
means and that BUGS does what you suggest, but I could be
misremembering or confusing the two systems.

- Bob

I thought that would be the case.

There might be a half-way house though. If I code my model in Stan and
then write the initialisation function in R, I often have to transform
between different parameterisations. Perhaps there could be some sort of
"parameter initialisation" block in Stan models so this wouldn't be
necessary. Sharing user-defined functions between this block and the
model could be useful. Also if custom initialisation is so useful for
good inference it would be nice to include the initialisations used with
the definition of the model.

>
> But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
> work, Stan would also be able to just converge.
>
> Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
> makes a big difference?  If so, we'd love to collect them as
> test cases.

You've hit the nail on the head, my examples have multi-modal
posteriors. I believe initialising from the prior allows the sampler to
have a much greater chance of visiting more of the modes. I'm trying to
learn a latent temporal variable that explains the data well. Each datum
has a latent pseudotime and the model's parameters are allowed to
smoothly vary over this pseudotime. The initialisation of the data
pseudotime parameters seems very important as Stan has trouble
reordering the data during sampling. I guess that's not the sort of
example you're looking for.

Regards,
John.

Most models I work with are described in terms of conditional distributions that have a natural order from hyperparameters through latent variables to data. I have had success initialising Stan using draws from the prior when the default "random" method didn't do so well. Are there any plans to incorporate some sort of initialisation like this? This would save users recoding their priors in init() functions (which can be error-prone).
> > Short answers: No and no.
> >
> > This has been something Andrew's been asking for, too.
> > But as is, Stan has no knowledge of any generative structure
> > in the model, so until we add a layer on top to deal with
> > directed graphical models or some more restricted class, we
> > don't have any hooks on which to hang such an implementation.
> I thought that would be the case.
>
> There might be a half-way house though. If I code my model in Stan and
> then write the initialisation function in R, I often have to transform
> between different parameterisations. Perhaps there could be some sort of
> "parameter initialisation" block in Stan models so this wouldn't be
> necessary. Sharing user-defined functions between this block and the
> model could be useful. Also if custom initialisation is so useful for
> good inference it would be nice to include the initialisations used with
> the definition of the model.

Hi John, just curious: have you found the diffuse starting points to be a problem in your models? Stan initializes all the unconstrained parameters i.i.d. uniform between -2 and 2 inclusive. When initializing from R, it should be an initialization on the constrained space. That is, if a parameter is declared as `real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;`, then it should be initialized between (0, 1).

What transformations are you doing between different parameterizations? Hopefully you're not trying to go from the constrained to the unconstrained space from R outside of Stan.

> >
> > But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
> > work, Stan would also be able to just converge.
> >
> > Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
> > makes a big difference?  If so, we'd love to collect them as
> > test cases.
> You've hit the nail on the head, my examples have multi-modal
> posteriors. I believe initialising from the prior allows the sampler to
> have a much greater chance of visiting more of the modes. I'm trying to
> learn a latent temporal variable that explains the data well. Each datum
> has a latent pseudotime and the model's parameters are allowed to
> smoothly vary over this pseudotime. The initialisation of the data
> pseudotime parameters seems very important as Stan has trouble
> reordering the data during sampling. I guess that's not the sort of
> example you're looking for.

It is an example of what we're looking for. Without knowing the details of your model: reordering is tough, multi-modality is tough. If specific initial values are putting Stan into a single mode, that's interesting to know and perhaps one of the future generations of Stan will be able to solve the problem without a hitch (I'm thinking Riemmanian manifold HMC). Of course, if it's really multi-modal and you're not trying to do a full Bayesian inference, that opens up a lot of doors that won't get you the right expectation, but might give you something from a high posterior mode.

>

>

> On 07/10/14 22:17, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>> On Oct 7, 2014, at 2:28 PM, John Reid <johnba...@gmail.com> wrote:

> If I code my model in Stan and
> then write the initialisation function in R, I often have to transform
> between different parameterisations.

Different parameterizations of the model in Stan?

The inits are always on the constrained scale.

> Perhaps there could be some sort of
> "parameter initialisation" block in Stan models so this wouldn't be
> necessary.

This is something that we had in the works before our adaptation
got a lot more robust.  We may still do it at some point.

>  Sharing user-defined functions between this block and the
> model could be useful.

Agreed.

We plan to add the transform functions as built-ins soon along with all of
our internal error checking.

> Also if custom initialisation is so useful for
> good inference

If custom initialization is really necessary, it may signal
a problem with inference in the model as Daniel pointed out.

> it would be nice to include the initialisations used with
> the definition of the model.

Definitely.

>> But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
>> work, Stan would also be able to just converge.
>>
>> Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
>> makes a big difference?  If so, we'd love to collect them as
>> test cases.

> You've hit the nail on the head, my examples have multi-modal
> posteriors. I believe initialising from the prior allows the sampler to
> have a much greater chance of visiting more of the modes.

That will depend on whether unconstraining uniform(-2,2) or
the prior is more dispersed and other factors about the posterior
curvature.

In any case, you may visit more, but it's going to be impossible
to do proper Bayesian inference in highly multimodal posteriors.

We'll be adding Michael Betancourt's thermodynamic sampling (arXiv-ed),
which will probably help with a lot of these issues.

We may also may wind up doing some kind of tempered optimization,
which may be more relevant for inference under multiple modes.

> I'm trying to
> learn a latent temporal variable that explains the data well. Each datum
> has a latent pseudotime and the model's parameters are allowed to
> smoothly vary over this pseudotime. The initialisation of the data
> pseudotime parameters seems very important as Stan has trouble
> reordering the data during sampling. I guess that's not the sort of
> example you're looking for.

These are the sorts of examples we're looking for.
Unfortunately, anything with modes separated by low density
troughs is going to be pretty much impossible to mix in
practice.  Like the mixture models in the manual:  K-means
clustering, HMMs, and LDA.  And even if you could mix, the
combinatorics will prevent proper posterior inference unless
one mode is so dominant the others can be ignored.

In this particular case, if the ordering is known, we have
a constrained parameter for ordered input.

- Bob

No, there is no way to get rid of error messages like this.
There have been a gazillion mails on this list about them
and opinions vary, but they're staying in for now.  (I've actually
been on the take-them-out side because I'm tired of responding
to all the mail we get about the message from new users.   The
current compromise is that they are not going to say "error"
anywhere in them in the next round.  If that doesn't work, we
may take more drastic measures in the future.)

The usual reason they occur is that discrete simulation of the Hamiltonian
needs to adapt its scales before it's numerically stable.  So you can
get these warnings even if you initialize with a draw from the posterior.

Adding an intercept to an ordered logistic can lead to non-identifiability
depending on what the model is.  For instance, if the cutpoints are
item-specific and the intercept is item-specific, you'll run into problems.
If one is fixed for each individual, then you still need to worry about
offsets, so you want to draw one with a prior with mean of 0.

- Bob

messages.subject: Multivariate count responses
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate count responses
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Imagine a dataset in which there are three response variables with count data. As a fun example, let's say you have a bag full of stale bread, and you have the option of feeding pieces of the bread to ducks in three kinds of places: (1) the pond, (2) the beach, and (3) the grass. Because you and others in the dataset have limited quantities of bread in your bags, we anticipate correlations between the responses -- once we account for the overall amount of bread, then as more pieces are thrown into the pond, we expect to see fewer pieces go to the beach and the grass, respectively. The dataset includes multiple observations of you and other benefactors of the ducks.

>From my vantage, these data would best be modeled as a multivariate Poisson response, but it is not clear yet that STAN can accommodate such models. Except for the literature on different kinds of crashes on highway segments (click <http://www.statistik.tuwien.ac.at/oezstat/ausg022-3/papers/tunaru.pdf> for an example), there seems to be relatively little attention to multiple responses of count data. Do you have advice on the possibilities of using STAN for this purpose? Are there examples of STAN modeling along these lines, whether for count data or multivariate discrete responses more generally?

Thanks!
- Jeremy

On Oct 8, 2014, at 4:14 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Really?  I thought we’d swiched this to be uniform from -0.5 to 0.5 as default, as we were having problems with some of the more extreme starting points.

I thought so, too, but we never did.

The problems with extreme starting points went away with
better adaptation and higher acceptance rates, so we left it
at [-2,2].

It's easy to specify with init = 0.5 in RStan.  The choice of 2
remains rather arbitrary.  It covers a lot of logit-scaled parameters
and runs from roughly 0.1 to 10.0 on positive constrained parameters,
and we thought that looked suitably diffuse for a default.

> Also, in response to the earlier question, it would not be possible for Stan to automatically draw parameters from the prior (indeed “the prior” is not so clearly defined, as all we are specifying is a joint density function) but it would be possible to do this “manually” by doing such simulations in R and then specifying these as starting values in the Stan call.

Once we add the prior/likelihood (aka base/delta split), this
should be easy for models with proper priors.

Of course, it'll introduce all the confusion about prior/likelihood
we've been trying to avoid, but that's inevitable with the above split.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can't install latest rstan!
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] can't install latest rstan!
messages.body_plain:
When the install script (`install_rstan`) calls `install.packages`, RStudio might prompt for whether you'd like to restart R prior to installing. When the user chooses the default option ("yes"), then R restarts and the packages install, but the rest of the script doesn't execute. Hence rstan isn't installed.

This happened to me initially, and I'd bet it's what happened to Andrew above (note that in his logs we see the result of install.packages("Rcpp", type = "source")but no output from the install script after that).

One option is to tell users to say "no" when they're asked about restarting R. I don't know if there are other/better options.

I haven't worked out exactly what conditions trigger the prompt to restart, but it's connected with whether the package is currently loaded. https://support.rstudio.com/hc/communities/public/questions/200652636-Suppress-restart-dialog-on-Loaded-Package-Install

On Oct 8, 2014, at 4:16 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

>
> On Oct 8, 2014, at 1:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>>
>> In any case, you may visit more, but it's going to be impossible
>> to do proper Bayesian inference in highly multimodal posteriors.
>
> "Impossible" is a bit strong.

When I say "highly multimodal", I'm talking about cases like LDA
or K-means clustering where the posterior multimodality is combinatorially
intractable (i.e., the number of modes grow exponentially and thus overwhelm any
hardware-based solution to explicitly sample from them).

> Let's just say that default Nuts (or Metropolis, or Gibbs, or HMC) will have problems with multimodal posteriors.

If someone could solve the combinatorial intractability problem,
we have bigger fish to fry than Bayesian sampling!

>> We'll be adding Michael Betancourt's thermodynamic sampling (arXiv-ed),
>> which will probably help with a lot of these issues.
>
> That's "adiabatic sampling" now!

So it is.  Michael even changed the title of the arXiv paper:

  http://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3489

>> Unfortunately, anything with modes separated by low density
>> troughs is going to be pretty much impossible to mix in
>> practice.
>
> Again, just to clarify:  "pretty much impossible to mix" using certain algorithms, maybe not with others.

Right.  Moving between a small number of modes is not intractable in
the same way that sampling from all of them is.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multivariate count responses
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multivariate count responses
messages.body_plain:
You could try a hierarchical model. You'd have three poisson
likelihoods (or neg binomial), each with a unique lambda that is
person-specific. The person-specific lambdas could be drawn from a
multivariate-normal distribution, which would account for the
correlations among observations within a person (you'd need to log the
lambda's or use Stan's logged poisson distribution). Thus, the data
are independent conditional on the person specific effects. I have a
fairly rough draft of a paper that does something similar. If you (or
others) are interested, I can send it back-channel.

Best,
Scott

messages.subject: Re: Multivariate count responses
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate count responses
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jeremy. Provided you don't know the amount of bread, then yeah, a multivariate Poisson makes sense.

A simple way to do this is the set up varying intercepts for pond/beach/grass, grouped by benefactor. Then plug those into the Poisson likelihoods to predict observable counts. The estimated covariance matrix for the varying effects should pick up your negative correlations, provided there is a hidden budget constraint.

On 08/10/14 14:44, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Hi John, just curious: have you found the diffuse starting points to
> be a problem in your models? Stan initializes all the unconstrained
> parameters i.i.d. uniform between -2 and 2 inclusive. When
> initializing from R, it should be an initialization on the constrained
> space. That is, if a parameter is declared as `real<lower=0,upper=1>
> theta;`, then it should be initialized between (0, 1).

What I have found is that if I sample from the prior then I find more
and better modes in the posterior of my model. I understand inference in
multimodal models is difficult and I would be very happy just to find
the best mode rather than samples from the posterior.

>
> What transformations are you doing between different
> parameterizations? Hopefully you're not trying to go from the
> constrained to the unconstrained space from R outside of Stan.

I wasn't clear enough: I meant different parameterisations of a
distribution, for instance R might parameterise a distribution using a
transformation of the parameters that Stan uses. No I'm not trying to
initialise in the unconstrained space.

Regards,
John.

Yes I understand that, I meant different parameterisations of a
distribution between Stan and R. E.g. the negative binomial has several
alternative parameterisations and switching between them in R and Stan

messages.subject: Causally restricted inference in time series
messages.subject_clean: Causally restricted inference in time series
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Users,
I am trying to build a Stan model for human temporal learning of properties perceptual stimuli, assuming that the observer is performing optimal inference.

In short, given a time series data_{1:N}, I am interested in inferring the 'conditional' posterior of a latent variable Sn after each data point P(S_n|data_{1:n}),  P(S_{n+1}|data_{1:n+1}),  P(S_{n+2}|data_{1:n+2}) etc. (Actual model attached. Could do with some vectorisation for speed-up).
I.e. an agent has to make a decision based on the posterior of Sn before receiving future data (causality).
This is opposed to getting the final posterior P(S_{1:N}|data_{1:N}) for which the posterior over S_n depends on the data received after time point n.

I could run the fitting of the model with data 1, with data 1:2, with data 1:3 ... but running Stan N(~1500) times seems extremely inefficient and slow (and speed matters in my application).

If I had an analytical expression of the posterior I could of course use an iterative approach (P(S_{n+1}|data_{1:n+1})=P(data_{n+1}|S_{n+1},data_n|)P(S_{n+1}|data_n)/Z (given a model of P(S_{n+1}|S_n) ), or similarly just updating the posterior.

Is there something equivalent that can be done in STAN,  or is there some way of writing out a model so that samples of S_n can be recorded before knowledge of data n+1 is used? (I have a feeling that I am just missing the right term to search for, sorry!)

Thanks for any comments!

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] power of a matrix
messages.body_plain:
JAGS could do this with an array to store intermediate
values:

  Q[1] <- original_Q %*% original_Q;
  for (n in 2:N)
    Q[n] <- original_Q %*% Q[n-1];

Then you'd get your result in Q[N] = original_Q^N.
And a whole lot of intermediate outputs you would not want
to monitor.

We spend a fair bit of time suggesting that people don't
literally translate JAGS code like the above to Stan but
to use reassignment.

We could certainly add a matrix power operator.  I added
a feature request, but did not assign it to anyone or make
it an immediate priority:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1073

I would suggest putting the loop in a function for the time
being.

functions {
  matrix matrix_pow(matrix a, int n) {
    if (n == 0)
      return diag_matrix(rep_vector(0, rows(a)));
    else if (n == 1)
      return a;
    else
      return a * matrix_pow(a, n - 1);
  }
}

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There's no way to directly implement what you're asking for
in Stan's object language given the way you've coded the model.
We treat all the parameters jointly and update them all
at the same time.

You could jam everything into a single model with parameters for
each data slice 1:N, but it wouldn't be pretty and it'd probably be slower
than running 1500 independent models and would definitely be a memory
hog.  Do you really need all 1500 predictions?

Or you could hope for conjugacy as you suggest, but then you
probably wouldn't need MCMC at all!

What you're looking for is related to the cut function in BUGS, but
I don't think cut would let you do what you need, either.

- Bob

We have a built-in ordered categorical that might be more
convenient.  We also have built-in ordered variables.  There's
nothing in your model that makes sure the cuts C are
ordered, which will likely be a problem.

I couldn't follow what your S variable was doing.  It looks
like you're using it to rescale differences, but that can easily
lead to multiplicative identities.  Change c and correspondingly
change S and you get the same value.

Using normal(0,100) or normal(0,1000) is not good in Stan unless
you really expect the variates to be on those scales.

If the model works in Stan and produces a reasonably high
n_eff per iteration, then it should be OK.

Rather than

 transpose(row(P,i)))

you can write

  P[i]'

messages.subject: Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to model ordinal data from a survey as a multivariate ordered logistic model. I am finding that as I increase the number of questions in the data (from 10 items to 16 items), the chains do not converge. The output for all of the chains in the 10 item dataset show convergence, but for the 16 item dataset, only 1 of the chains converge.

The underlying latent parameter for the questions are modelled as a multivariate normal distribution, and each integer response as an ordered logistic. I am modelling the prior for the cutpoints for each item as a fixed-scaled cumulative sum of a symmetric dirichlet. For identifiability, I set the first cutpoint to 0. I am running on CmdStan (v2.4), Linux Ubuntu.

Do you have any suggestions for choices of priors or scales that might help convergence? My eventual goal is to include all the data, which is 56 questions.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identification of multinomial (by means of Poisson) IRT/ideal point model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Identification of multinomial (by means of Poisson) IRT/ideal point model
messages.body_plain:
On Oct 9, 2014, at 2:42 PM, Thomas <daub...@tcd.ie> wrote:

> I’m fitting a multinomial (by means of Poisson) IRT/ideal point model for category counts in policy documents with
>
> Count(document, category) ~ Poisson(exp(alpha_doc + psi_cat + beta_cat*theta_doc))
>
> As constraints, one psi and one beta are set to zero, and the ideal points theta receive a standard normal prior. A conditional statement based on the order of two betas is used to reverse the scale when necessary (I know that half-normal priors might be better for that, but I had mixed experiences when working with those).

I'm curious what the mixed experience was.  Did you
constrain the parameters to be positive?  The log transform on the
variables does change the posterior geometry and hence affects
sampling.

> It seems that the constraints are sufficient to identify the model, at least I get very similar results across different runs.

That does sound sufficient to identify the model.

> It seems to work since the standard normal prior on the ideal points theta apparently leads to a standard normal posterior distribution of the ideal points. Is there a simple answer why this happens?

Yes.  When you have too many degrees of freedom in the parameterization (i.e.,
non-identifiability), what happens is that one parameter can go up
or down in scale or shift in location, with a corresponding shift or scaling
of another parameter group without affecting the posterior
density.   By assigning one group of variables a normal(0,1) prior, that
identifies the scale and location that's going to fit best, hence you
get normal(0,1) posteriors for the constrained variable and everything else
floats.

There's a discussion in the Gelman and Hill's book section on (multilevel)
IRT and ideal-point models.

> I would not necessarily have expected that, and when I code the same model in Jags, theta does not come out standardized in the posterior and the model lacks identification.

My guess would be that either (a) it's not exactly the same model in
JAGS, or (b) you haven't run JAGS long enough to converge.
Gibbs sampling is slow to converge if you have correlations in the posterior,
as you do in these essentially unidentified models.

> Is it ok to rely on the prior doing the job in Stan or would it still be better to standardize the ideal points deterministically (probably at the expense of speed?)? Any hints appreciated.

It is critical to rely on the prior or another means of
identification of the model in Stan.  Just standardizing the
resulting parameter draws won't work.  There's a discussion
of the issue for a very simple example with posterior draws
in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual, with
more explanation about what's going on and why the post-standardization
seems to work in Gibbs (as far as I know, nobody's shown it gives
the right answer formally, though Andrew's convinced it does), but
not in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

- Bob

messages.subject: Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
messages.subject_clean: Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

At present, STAN samples all parameters at every iteration.

In some cases, it may be useful to partition the parameters into "fast" and "slow" subsets, where fast parameters are quick to update, whilst slow parameters are not.  The logic here is that you might only update the slow parameters every N iterations.

As an example, consider Gaussian Process Regression, where a training set is used to make predictions for a prediction set.  Full Bayes (and therefore full MCMC) is slow because the hyperparameters are expensive to optimise/sample from.  One alternative to this is to use empirical Bayes, whereby I set the hyperparameters to their maximum a posteriori (MAP) values, and then just sample from the GP as desired.

I see two possibilities here:
1) STAN could be programmed to optimise some parameters (eg hyperparameters) whilst sampling others.  I don't know how difficult such a mixed implementation would be, but certainly there is an element of Gibbs-like sampling here (the sampled parameters will be sampled conditional on the values of the optmised parameters); or
2) You might only update the hyperparameters every N iterations.  Then, you can get significantly more samples from the "fast" predictions.

The second case is effectively a half-way house between empirical Bayes and MCMC - you get somewhat more realistic confidence intervals, and faster running times than full MCMC, assuming that your hyperparameters are close to the MAP values.

Is something like this interesting? Is it feasible?  For the speed gain to be realised here, STAN would need to know not to calculate the derivatives of "slow" parameters at specified iterations.

Thoughts?

Thanks
Julian

> > Speaking more generally about how Stan is structured:  Currently it only allows jumping through the full space of parameters.  But we are planning to implement a partition of parameter space so that it can jump on one set of parameters with the others set at fixed values.
> >
> > A
> >
> > On Oct 9, 2014, at 7:57 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Hello all,
> > >
> > > At present, STAN samples all parameters at every iteration.
> > >
> > > In some cases, it may be useful to partition the parameters into "fast" and "slow" subsets, where fast parameters are quick to update, whilst slow parameters are not.  The logic here is that you might only update the slow parameters every N iterations.
> > >
> > > As an example, consider Gaussian Process Regression, where a training set is used to make predictions for a prediction set.  Full Bayes (and therefore full MCMC) is slow because the hyperparameters are expensive to optimise/sample from.  One alternative to this is to use variational Bayes, whereby I set the hyperparameters to their maximum a posteriori (MAP) values, and then just sample from the GP as desired.
> > >
> > > I see two possibilities here:
> > > 1) STAN could be programmed to optimise some parameters (eg hyperparameters) whilst sampling others.  I don't know how difficult such a mixed implementation would be, but certainly there is an element of Gibbs-like sampling here (the sampled parameters will be sampled conditional on the values of the optmised parameters); or
> > > 2) You might only update the hyperparameters every N iterations.  Then, you can get significantly more samples from the "fast" predictions.
> > >
> > > The second case is effectively a half-way house between variational Bayes and MCMC - you get somewhat more realistic confidence intervals, and faster running times than full MCMC, assuming that your hyperparameters are close to the MAP values.
> > >
> > > Is something like this interesting? Is it feasible?  For the speed gain to be realised here, STAN would need to know not to calculate the derivatives of "slow" parameters at specified iterations.
> > >
> > > Thoughts?
> > >
> > > Thanks
> > > Julian
> > >

Oh, Bob! I think you were looking at my original model in my very first post, instead of the new one that I attached in my last post. All of the issues you mentioned have already been taken care of in this new one. Here I attach the file again. And also paste the code as below.

--- START ---

library(rstan)

rm(list = ls())

code <- '  // STAN: hierarchical ordered logistic model
data {
  int<lower=0> N;  // number of objects
  int<lower=1> K;  // number of categories
  int<lower=1> L;  // number of groups
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];  // response
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] sex;  // predictor
  vector<lower=1>[N] age;  // predictor
  int<lower=1,upper=L> group[N];  // group level predictor
}
parameters {
  vector[L] alpha;  // intercept
  real muAlpha;  // mu for intercept
  real<lower=0> sigmaAlpha;  // sigma for intercept
  real beta1;  // slope for sex
  real beta2;  // slope for age
  ordered[K-1] c;  // cutpoints for ordered logistic model
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] y_hat;

  for (i in 1:N)

    y_hat[i] <- alpha[group[i]] + beta1 * sex[i] + beta2 * age[i];
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(y_hat[n], c);
//  y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[n] * beta, c);
//  increment_log_prob(ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c));
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  for (n in 1:N)
    log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], y_hat[n], c);
//  log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c);
}
'

N <- 100  # number of objects
K <- 4  # number of categories
L <- 10  # number of groups
y <- sample(1:K, N, replace = T)
group <- sample(1:L, N, replace = T)
sex <- sample(0:1, N, replace = T)
age <- sample(50:100, N, replace = T)

dataList <- c("N", "K", "L", "y", "group", "sex", "age")
model <- stan_model(model_code = code, model_name='ordered_logitistic', verbose=FALSE)
fit <- sampling(model, data = dataList, iter = 1000, chains = 4)

waic <- function(stanfit){
  loglik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
  n1 <- nrow(loglik)  # number of samples
  n2 <- ncol(loglik)  # number of data points
  vars <- colSums((loglik - matrix(colMeans(loglik), n1, n2, byrow = T))^2) / (n1 - 1)
  pwaic <- sum(vars)  # effective parameter number
  lpd <- sum(log(colMeans(exp(loglik))))  # log pointwise predictive density
  waic <- -2 * (lpd - pwaic)
  return(list(WAIC = waic, Pwaic = pwaic, LPD = lpd))
}

print(waic(fit))

---END---

Looks OK to me.

You don't need to store the y_hat, but you can.

Ordered logistic hasn't been extended to vectors yet, so

parameterization here:

That is, take

  alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1);

and define as either a local variable or a transformed
parameter,

  alpha <- muAlpha + sigmaAlpha * alpha_raw;

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob, I am happy the model looks OK.

There are 2 itchy things on me.

1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.
2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
messages.body_plain:
Getting more samples by freezing more expensive hyper parameters does absolutely
nothing for you as p (fast | slow) != p (fast) = \int dslow p(fast, slow).  In particular,
the conditional distribution drastically underestimates the true marginal uncertainty
of the fast parameters.  There are various ways to estimate p(fast | slow) but none
of them can get around the ultimate lack of utility of the conditional distribution for
inference.

P.S. STAN should be Stan

On Oct 10, 2014, at 12:57 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello all,
>
> At present, STAN samples all parameters at every iteration.
>
> In some cases, it may be useful to partition the parameters into "fast" and "slow" subsets, where fast parameters are quick to update, whilst slow parameters are not.  The logic here is that you might only update the slow parameters every N iterations.
>
> As an example, consider Gaussian Process Regression, where a training set is used to make predictions for a prediction set.  Full Bayes (and therefore full MCMC) is slow because the hyperparameters are expensive to optimise/sample from.  One alternative to this is to use variational Bayes, whereby I set the hyperparameters to their maximum a posteriori (MAP) values, and then just sample from the GP as desired.
>
> I see two possibilities here:
> 1) STAN could be programmed to optimise some parameters (eg hyperparameters) whilst sampling others.  I don't know how difficult such a mixed implementation would be, but certainly there is an element of Gibbs-like sampling here (the sampled parameters will be sampled conditional on the values of the optmised parameters); or
> 2) You might only update the hyperparameters every N iterations.  Then, you can get significantly more samples from the "fast" predictions.
>
> The second case is effectively a half-way house between variational Bayes and MCMC - you get somewhat more realistic confidence intervals, and faster running times than full MCMC, assuming that your hyperparameters are close to the MAP values.
>
> Is something like this interesting? Is it feasible?  For the speed gain to be realised here, STAN would need to know not to calculate the derivatives of "slow" parameters at specified iterations.
>
> Thoughts?
>
> Thanks
> Julian
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I wasn't aware that I could use an array to do this in JAGS (I'm almost as new to JAGS as I am to Stan). Here is the JAGS code that worked, with the help of a local user (QW is the original 4x4 matrix, QWt[t, 1:4, 1:4]  is QW^t):

          QWt[1, 1:4, 1:4] <- QW
          for (gen in 2:t) { QWt[gen, 1:4, 1:4] <- QW %*% QWt[gen - 1, 1:4, 1:4] }

Many thanks for your help,
Paul

On Thursday, October 9, 2014 6:18:27 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> JAGS could do this with an array to store intermediate
> values:
>
>   Q[1] <- original_Q %*% original_Q;
>   for (n in 2:N)
>     Q[n] <- original_Q %*% Q[n-1];
>
> Then you'd get your result in Q[N] = original_Q^N.
> And a whole lot of intermediate outputs you would not want
> to monitor.
>
> We spend a fair bit of time suggesting that people don't
> literally translate JAGS code like the above to Stan but
> to use reassignment.
>
> We could certainly add a matrix power operator.  I added
> a feature request, but did not assign it to anyone or make
> it an immediate priority:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1073
>
> I would suggest putting the loop in a function for the time
> being.
>
> functions {
>   matrix matrix_pow(matrix a, int n) {
>     if (n == 0)
>       return diag_matrix(rep_vector(0, rows(a)));
>     else if (n == 1)
>       return a;
>     else
>       return a * matrix_pow(a, n - 1);
>   }
> }
>
>
> - Bob

On Oct 10, 2014, at 1:12 AM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks Bob, I am happy the model looks OK.
>
> There are 2 itchy things on me.
>
> 1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.

You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.

A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
that's non-zero for members of that group.  You can identify with
a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
are estimated relative to it.

> 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.

That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).

You may also need to give c a prior.

- Bob

>

>

> parameterization here:

>

>

On Oct 10, 2014, at 2:54 PM, Erikson Kaszubowski <erik...@yahoo.com.br> wrote:

> Dear Professor Gelman,
>
> I missed your call for Stan research stories, but the recent post about stranded dolphins mentioned it again.
>
> When I read about the Crowdstorming project in your blog (http://andrewgelman.com/2014/04/28/crowdstorming-dataset/), I thought it would be a good project to apply my recent studies in bayesian modeling.
>
> The project coordinators shared a big dataset (with 124,621 cases) and each research team had to independently analyze the data and answer two research questions:
> 1) Are soccer referees more likely to give red cards to dark skin toned players?
> 2) Do referees from countries with high skin tone bias are more likely to be biased towards dark skin toned players?
>
> Given the data structure (each case is a player-referee dyad, with variables about how many games occurred between them and more) and inpired by the recent reading of ARM, I thought a Multilevel Binomial-Normal Regression could be a good model to analyze the data.
>
> I initially created a JAGS model that only worked in small samples of the dataset. When I tried to analyze the whole thing, JAGS couldn't get off the ground. So, I decided to give Stan a try... And it worked like a charm!
>
> The project article is still being written, but all analyses are already published in the Open Science Framework. Here's the link for my analysis:
>
> https://osf.io/6zvqy/
>
> A short report, source codes and Stan chains are all there, in case anyone is interested.
>
> I know the model isn't such a great novelty and there is plenty of criticism to be done about what I did.
> But we can say, at least, that when people first crowdstormed a dataset, Stan was there!
>
> Thank you and all the Stan team for such a great tool!
>
> Best regards,
> Erikson Kaszubowski
>
>

messages.body_plain:
If a categorial id is not appropriate as a regression predictor, you want to change the example code in this link: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.12/radon_group.stan

In this file, the county id is obviously categorial but defined as int and used as a regression predictor.

On Friday, October 10, 2014 4:44:52 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On Oct 10, 2014, at 1:12 AM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Thanks Bob, I am happy the model looks OK.
> >
> > There are 2 itchy things on me.
> >
> > 1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.
>
> You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.
>
> A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
> that's non-zero for members of that group.  You can identify with
> a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
> are estimated relative to it.
>
> > 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.
>
> That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
> can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).
>
> You may also need to give c a prior.
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > On Friday, October 10, 2014 1:00:20 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Looks OK to me.
> >
> > You don't need to store the y_hat, but you can.
> >
> > Ordered logistic hasn't been extended to vectors yet, so
> > you can't speed that up.
> >
> > The only thing I can see to try would be a non-centered
> > parameterization here:
> >
> > >   alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
> >
> >
> > That is, take
> >
> >   alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1);
> >
> > and define as either a local variable or a transformed
> > parameter,
> >
> >   alpha <- muAlpha + sigmaAlpha * alpha_raw;
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Oct 9, 2014, at 10:24 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Oh, Bob! I think you were looking at my original model in my very first post, instead of the new one that I attached in my last post. All of the issues you mentioned have already been taken care of in this new one. Here I attach the file again. And also paste the code as below.
> > >
> > > --- START ---
> > >
> > > library(rstan)
> > >
> > > rm(list = ls())
> > >
> > > code <- '  // STAN: hierarchical ordered logistic model
> > > data {
> > >   int<lower=0> N;  // number of objects
> > >   int<lower=1> K;  // number of categories
> > >   int<lower=1> L;  // number of groups
> > >   int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];  // response
> > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] sex;  // predictor
> > >   vector<lower=1>[N] age;  // predictor
> > >   int<lower=1,upper=L> group[N];  // group level predictor
> > > }

> > >   vector[L] alpha;  // intercept

> > >   real beta1;  // slope for sex
> > >   real beta2;  // slope for age
> > >   ordered[K-1] c;  // cutpoints for ordered logistic model
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >   vector[N] y_hat;
> > >   for (i in 1:N)
> > >     y_hat[i] <- alpha[group[i]] + beta1 * sex[i] + beta2 * age[i];
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >   alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
> > >   for (n in 1:N)
> > >     y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(y_hat[n], c);
> > > //  y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[n] * beta, c);
> > > //  increment_log_prob(ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c));
> > > }
> > > generated quantities {
> > >   vector[N] log_lik;
> > >   for (n in 1:N)
> > >     log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], y_hat[n], c);
> > > //  log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c);
> > > }
> > > '
> > >
> > > N <- 100  # number of objects
> > > K <- 4  # number of categories
> > > L <- 10  # number of groups
> > > y <- sample(1:K, N, replace = T)
> > > group <- sample(1:L, N, replace = T)
> > > sex <- sample(0:1, N, replace = T)
> > > age <- sample(50:100, N, replace = T)
> > >
> > > dataList <- c("N", "K", "L", "y", "group", "sex", "age")
> > > model <- stan_model(model_code = code, model_name='ordered_logitistic', verbose=FALSE)
> > > fit <- sampling(model, data = dataList, iter = 1000, chains = 4)
> > >
> > > waic <- function(stanfit){
> > >   loglik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
> > >   n1 <- nrow(loglik)  # number of samples
> > >   n2 <- ncol(loglik)  # number of data points
> > >   vars <- colSums((loglik - matrix(colMeans(loglik), n1, n2, byrow = T))^2) / (n1 - 1)
> > >   pwaic <- sum(vars)  # effective parameter number
> > >   lpd <- sum(log(colMeans(exp(loglik))))  # log pointwise predictive density
> > >   waic <- -2 * (lpd - pwaic)
> > >   return(list(WAIC = waic, Pwaic = pwaic, LPD = lpd))
> > > }
> > >
> > > print(waic(fit))
> > >

> > > > On Wednesday, October 8, 2014 1:40:36 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > No, there is no way to get rid of error messages like this.

> > > > and opinions vary, but they're staying in for now.  (I've actually

> > > >
