messages.body_plain:
No.  Unless I’m misunderstanding something here, county id in this example is used as an indexing variable, _not_ as a regression predictor.  The model has b[county[i]].  If it had b*county[i], then county id would be a regression predictor.  b[county[i]] is just fine.
A

On Oct 10, 2014, at 11:20 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

> If a categorial id is not appropriate as a regression predictor, you want to change the example code in this link: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.12/radon_group.stan
>
> In this file, the county id is obviously categorial but defined as int and used as a regression predictor.
>
> On Friday, October 10, 2014 4:44:52 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > On Oct 10, 2014, at 1:12 AM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Thanks Bob, I am happy the model looks OK.
> > >
> > > There are 2 itchy things on me.
> > >
> > > 1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.
> >
> > You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.
> >
> > A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
> > that's non-zero for members of that group.  You can identify with
> > a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
> > are estimated relative to it.
> >
> > > 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.
> >
> > That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
> > can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).
> >
> > You may also need to give c a prior.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > >
> > > On Friday, October 10, 2014 1:00:20 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > Looks OK to me.
> > >
> > > You don't need to store the y_hat, but you can.
> > >
> > > Ordered logistic hasn't been extended to vectors yet, so
> > > you can't speed that up.
> > >
> > > The only thing I can see to try would be a non-centered
> > > parameterization here:
> > >
> > > >   alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
> > >
> > >
> > > That is, take
> > >
> > >   alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1);
> > >
> > > and define as either a local variable or a transformed
> > > parameter,
> > >
> > >   alpha <- muAlpha + sigmaAlpha * alpha_raw;
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > On Oct 9, 2014, at 10:24 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Oh, Bob! I think you were looking at my original model in my very first post, instead of the new one that I attached in my last post. All of the issues you mentioned have already been taken care of in this new one. Here I attach the file again. And also paste the code as below.
> > > >
> > > > --- START ---
> > > >
> > > > library(rstan)
> > > >
> > > > rm(list = ls())
> > > >
> > > > code <- '  // STAN: hierarchical ordered logistic model
> > > > data {
> > > >   int<lower=0> N;  // number of objects
> > > >   int<lower=1> K;  // number of categories
> > > >   int<lower=1> L;  // number of groups
> > > >   int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];  // response
> > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] sex;  // predictor
> > > >   vector<lower=1>[N] age;  // predictor
> > > >   int<lower=1,upper=L> group[N];  // group level predictor
> > > > }
> > > > parameters {
> > > >   vector[L] alpha;  // intercept
> > > >   real muAlpha;  // mu for intercept
> > > >   real<lower=0> sigmaAlpha;  // sigma for intercept
> > > >   real beta1;  // slope for sex
> > > >   real beta2;  // slope for age
> > > >   ordered[K-1] c;  // cutpoints for ordered logistic model
> > > > }
> > > > transformed parameters {
> > > >   vector[N] y_hat;
> > > >   for (i in 1:N)
> > > >     y_hat[i] <- alpha[group[i]] + beta1 * sex[i] + beta2 * age[i];
> > > > }
> > > > model {
> > > >   alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
> > > >   for (n in 1:N)
> > > >     y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(y_hat[n], c);
> > > > //  y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[n] * beta, c);
> > > > //  increment_log_prob(ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c));
> > > > }
> > > > generated quantities {
> > > >   vector[N] log_lik;
> > > >   for (n in 1:N)
> > > >     log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], y_hat[n], c);
> > > > //  log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c);
> > > > }
> > > > '
> > > >
> > > > N <- 100  # number of objects
> > > > K <- 4  # number of categories
> > > > L <- 10  # number of groups
> > > > y <- sample(1:K, N, replace = T)
> > > > group <- sample(1:L, N, replace = T)
> > > > sex <- sample(0:1, N, replace = T)
> > > > age <- sample(50:100, N, replace = T)
> > > >
> > > > dataList <- c("N", "K", "L", "y", "group", "sex", "age")
> > > > model <- stan_model(model_code = code, model_name='ordered_logitistic', verbose=FALSE)
> > > > fit <- sampling(model, data = dataList, iter = 1000, chains = 4)
> > > >
> > > > waic <- function(stanfit){
> > > >   loglik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
> > > >   n1 <- nrow(loglik)  # number of samples
> > > >   n2 <- ncol(loglik)  # number of data points
> > > >   vars <- colSums((loglik - matrix(colMeans(loglik), n1, n2, byrow = T))^2) / (n1 - 1)
> > > >   pwaic <- sum(vars)  # effective parameter number
> > > >   lpd <- sum(log(colMeans(exp(loglik))))  # log pointwise predictive density
> > > >   waic <- -2 * (lpd - pwaic)
> > > >   return(list(WAIC = waic, Pwaic = pwaic, LPD = lpd))
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > print(waic(fit))
> > > >
> > > > ---END---

> > > > lead to multiplicative identities.  Change c and correspondingly
> > > > change S and you get the same value.
> > > >
> > > > Using normal(0,100) or normal(0,1000) is not good in Stan unless
> > > > you really expect the variates to be on those scales.
> > > >
> > > > If the model works in Stan and produces a reasonably high
> > > > n_eff per iteration, then it should be OK.
> > > >
> > > > Rather than
> > > >
> > > >  transpose(row(P,i)))

> > > > > In my model, intercepts were modeled as a mixed effect with a normal dist based on a group level predictor, which was simply the group id. So, intercept essentially has a predictor in my case. On the other hand, c would be item-specific with a non-constrained prior. Would the non-identibability issue still legit in my case? Also, did you mean I need to set the prior for intercepts' mean as 0 and this would get around the problem?
> > > > >
> > > > > Please take a look of my working ordered logistic model with stan, which also includes a fit on simulated data and waic implementation. Hopefully the coding is clear enough for you to catch any improper.
> > > > >
> > > > > So much appreciations.

> > > > > On Wednesday, October 8, 2014 1:40:36 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > No, there is no way to get rid of error messages like this.
> > > > > There have been a gazillion mails on this list about them
> > > > > and opinions vary, but they're staying in for now.  (I've actually
> > > > > been on the take-them-out side because I'm tired of responding
> > > > > to all the mail we get about the message from new users.   The
> > > > > current compromise is that they are not going to say "error"
> > > > > anywhere in them in the next round.  If that doesn't work, we
> > > > > may take more drastic measures in the future.)
> > > > >
> > > > > The usual reason they occur is that discrete simulation of the Hamiltonian
> > > > > needs to adapt its scales before it's numerically stable.  So you can
> > > > > get these warnings even if you initialize with a draw from the posterior.
> > > > >
> > > > > Adding an intercept to an ordered logistic can lead to non-identifiability
> > > > > depending on what the model is.  For instance, if the cutpoints are
> > > > > item-specific and the intercept is item-specific, you'll run into problems.
> > > > > If one is fixed for each individual, then you still need to worry about
> > > > > offsets, so you want to draw one with a prior with mean of 0.
> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob
> > > > >
> > > > > On Oct 8, 2014, at 4:47 AM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.body_plain:
It depends on what you mean by "Bayesian".  You can
think of point estimates as a kind of approximate Bayesian
inference, especially if you consider things like using
curvature to do a Laplace approximation of posterior uncertainty.
You can think of techniques like EM and VB
as slightly less crude approximations.  "Full Bayes", as it's
often known, means using the full posterior for inference.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Difficulties with lkj_corr
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, October 14, 2014 9:33:32 PM UTC-4, Markian Pahuta wrote:
> My model runs when the parameters Omega_prior and Omega_study are a diagonal matrix of 1 (uncomment variable definition in data block, and comment in parameter block).
>
> When I run the model using the lkj distribution I get the error:
> > Error in function stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): yy is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1:0.Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
> > Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

You can circumvent this error by commenting out

Omega_prior ~ lkj_corr(1);
Omega_study ~ lkj_corr(1);

if your shape parameter is 1, then this prior is uniform over positive definite correlation matrices. So it doesn't affect the posterior in principle, although the function has to check whether the matrix is in fact positive definite, which is numerically fallible even though a declared correlation matrix will be positive definite by construction in Stan. However, I would guess that this is a symptom of a problem with your .stan program, rather than the problem itself.

Probably unrelated, but we do want to push people toward expressing their models in terms of a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, rather than declaring a correlation matrix in the parameters block. That avoids a lot of numerical problems and can be a lot faster. See the cholesky_factor_corr type and the lkj_cholesky_corr(1) density, because you do have to register the prior explicitly when dealing with the Cholesky factor.

> When I define the Omega_ parameters simply as matrices (not corr_matrix), I get the error:
> > Error in function stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): yy is not symmetric. y[0,1] is 1.2277783349104863:0, but y[1,0] element is -1.2975:0Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
> > Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

That won't work for the reason you encountered: It isn't a symmetric matrix so it can't be a correlation matrix.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The declarations need to be as corr_matrix, but even so,
Stan will run into trouble in high dimensions due to the
transform from unconstrained parameters and/or the
solver.  If your correlation matrices are less than
10 dimensional, I don't see why it wouldn't at least
initialize as you wrote it (given that it works with
hard-coded unit correlation matrices).

But having said all that, what you really want to do for something
like this is follow Ben Goodrich's advice, which I've
written up for the 2.5 manual (attached).  The final coding we recommend is
in the "Optimization through Cholesky Factorization" section.
I just realized in first introducing the model I should point
to this implementation, as it should be a lot faster and a lot
more stable arithmetically.

We're also not recommending very diffuse (inverse) gamma
priors like BUGS has in its example models, but I don't know
what your gam_shape or gam_rate values are.  I'm just writing
up Andrew's advice on those in another section for the 2.5 manual.

- Bob

P.S.  And if you haven't built up to this complicated model through
      simpler models, I'd suggest doing that.

messages.body_plain:
I got the idea for setting the cut point prior as fixed-scaled cumulative sum of a dirichlet from this thread:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/2YMo3SUzHTg/jgeoyZfUSBsJ

When the cutpoints have a non-informative prior, I found it was extremely slow to converge (over 10 times as long) versus setting a more informative prior. However, looking at the older thread, the poster seems to have convergence issues as well in some of the chains with this approach.

I'm definitely not an expert, but I have found that constraining the prior helps with non-identifiability issues and convergence speed. You might want to put a broad prior, even a normal(0,10) or cauchy(0,10) (for longer tails) on muAlpha and sigmaAlpha.

messages.subject: Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.subject_clean: Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Stan is very useful because of its flexibility as an MCMC langauge.  It is possible to get something working quickly and reasonably effectively because the user has to express intentions in a fairly high-level way, whilst all the difficult sampling is taken care of. The more useful Stan can be in a wider range of situations, the better.

One of the reasons why one might move away from Stan to custom code is because the problem is "too hard" in some sense - perhaps the number of data points is too large and requires special techniques.  Perhaps there are linear algebra operations which scale as some poor function of the number of data points.  Gaussian Process methods are the best example of this, where naive implementations scale as O(N^3).

Perhaps it is useful to start a wishlist of features which can help extend the usefulness of Stan in this way, by making it feasible to a wider range of problems.

In the context of Gaussian Process regression, there are a number of ways of getting around the O(N^3) method, but one way is the use of a conjugate gradient approximation to find the approximate inverse of the covariance matrix.  Perhaps a Stan function which finds the approximate matrix inverse of a matrix C would be useful, eg approxinverse(matrix C, tolerance e), where e is the fractional tolerance.   If you are sampling the hyperparameters as well, you will need a way of getting the determinant of the covariance matrix fast as well, or the call to multi_normal will spend O(N^3) time calculating the determinant.

Any other thoughts?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Suppose there are two sets of data: training data {y_train, x_train} and testing data {y_test, x_test}. I am trying to understand how to obtain posterior predictive distribution for y_test given x_test and a model estimated using the training data.

I find the wells_predicted.stan <https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.5/wells_predicted.stan> example relevant. If I understand it correctly. its generated quantities section provides posterior distribution for y_train. To obtain the posterior distribution for y_test (the unseen data), I am wondering if I just need to declare testing data {y_test, x_test} in the data section and loop over the testing data in the generated quantities as the example code does.

Another question I have related to the following quote from the stan 2.4 manual (pp 340, Predictive Inference):

[start quote]
p(y_tilde | y) = integrate_Θ p(y_tilde|θ) p(θ|y) dθ
Here, both the original constants and predictors x and the new constants and predictors x_tilde are implicit.
[end quote]

Can anyone explain why the the new constants and predictors x_tilde has to be implicit? Is it just to simplify the notation here or we don't normally consider new constants and predictors in predictive inference?

Thanks for any suggestions,
Yu-Kai

messages.subject: Pystan: Thinning Causes Segmentation Fault
messages.subject_clean: Pystan: Thinning Causes Segmentation Fault
messages.body_plain: I used to be able to thin my model fits in Pystan and it worked like expected. However, I recently upgraded to Xcode 6 on OS X Mavericks. When I did so, it broke my install of Pystan. I deleted Pystan, reinstalled the new command line tools for Xcode 6, and reinstalled Pystan (2.4.0.3). Now, Pystan/STAN runs like expected unless I try to thin. When I try to thin the posterior samples, the model compiles and runs fine. However, when I try to work with the fit, such as trace plots or extracting coefficients, I get a Segmentation Fault 11 error that crashes Python, which I believe is a memory issue. This happens whether I thin by 5 or 20 and whether I have 1,000 or 100,000 iterations. Why does thinning now cause a memory issue that crashed Python? Did the upgrade to Xcode 6 change something?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Integer vector and matrix
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Integer vector and matrix
messages.body_plain:
Is there a reason you can't declare D1 as a matrix of
reals?  You can assign integer values to real variables.
All the code you sent does is multiply the integers by
reals, which is going to implicitly promote the integers
to reals before multiplying anyway.

data :: matrix[N,K] D1;
parameter :: vector[K] a;
parameter :: vector[N] d1;
transformed parameter :: matrix[N,K] phi1;

    for (i in 1:N1){
        for (j in 1:K){
            phi1[i,j] <- (D1[i,j]*a[j]) / d1[i];
        }
    }

As to the matrix issue, you're not doing matrix algebra
here, you're doing elementwise operations.  You could remove
one loop and use the elementwise product operator ".*":

for (i in 1:N1)

  phi[i] <- (D[i] .* a) / d1[i]

But I don't see any way to remove both loops.

And doing it with ".*" won't be any faster because there's no
savings to be had in eliminating shared computation or storage
for derivatives, which are all compltely independent in
elementwise products..

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difficulties with lkj_corr
messages.body_plain:
If a is a matrix, then a[n] is the n-th *row* vector.
That's why we can write a linear regression as:

  y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma);

or as

  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta, sigma);

where y is a vector, x the data matrix, and beta the
coefficient vector.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
messages.body_plain:
We don't (yet) have any default recommendations for priors on
cutpoints.

The main issue you have to deal with is making sure you
don't have multiplicative (scale) or additive (location)
identifiability issues with the cutpoints and a regression.

If you give the regression a mean and the cutpoints float,
then you have a classic non-identifiability problem.  You
can pin the value of one of the cutpoints to identify the
location.  Then if you still need to worry about identifying
the scales.

- Bob

On Oct 15, 2014, at 6:40 PM, Yu-Kai Lin <ykl...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Suppose there are two sets of data: training data {y_train, x_train} and testing data {y_test, x_test}. I am trying to understand how to obtain posterior predictive distribution for y_test given x_test and a model estimated using the training data.
>
> I find the wells_predicted.stan example relevant. If I understand it correctly. its generated quantities section provides posterior distribution for y_train. To obtain the posterior distribution for y_test (the unseen data), I am wondering if I just need to declare testing data {y_test, x_test} in the data section and loop over the testing data in the generated quantities as the example code does.
>

Yes.

There's a section in the manual titled "Prediction, Forecasting, and Backcasting"
in the regression chapter of the manual.

You can also do the predictions in the model block if they're too complicated
to do with simple random number generators.  It's just more efficient to put
them in generated quantities.

> Another question I have related to the following quote from the stan 2.4 manual (pp 340, Predictive Inference):
>
> [start quote]
> p(y_tilde | y) = integrate_Θ p(y_tilde|θ) p(θ|y) dθ
> Here, both the original constants and predictors x and the new constants and predictors x_tilde are implicit.
> [end quote]
>
> Can anyone explain why the the new constants and predictors x_tilde has to be implicit? Is it just to simplify the notation here or we don't normally consider new constants and predictors in predictive inference?

Yes, just to simplify notation.  The manual follows the notation in
the early parts of Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis book.  I should
just go in and make the x explicit to avoid any confusion.  We did that in
the very beginning of the Stan manual, which also used to drop the x.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.subject_clean: Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julian,

I think this is a great discussion to have, and I would add to the list the ability to optimize for models with "blocky" conditional independence structures.

I've encountered this in non-linear hierarchical regression models, where bottom level parameters in different groups are defined to be conditionally independent of each other, yet Stan cannot know about this structure and may do unnecessary gradient computations.  It's tempting to use a Gibbs sampler in such cases, but of course it's still valuable to do joint transitions between the hyperparameters and lower level parameters that do have dependencies.

I'm not sure if this has been discussed on the list already, perhaps we've touched on it here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#%21searchin/stan-users/conditionally$20independent$20blocks/stan-users/uHvT2Weq73I/49KoRSpOLhgJ>.  I know Michael B. has thought about this and may be able to weigh in with a better description of the problem or comments on whether or not it's worth further discussion.

Best,

~Nathan

On Wednesday, October 15, 2014 6:17:28 PM UTC-4, Julian King wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> Stan is very useful because of its flexibility as an MCMC langauge.  It is possible to get something working quickly and reasonably effectively because the user has to express intentions in a fairly high-level way, whilst all the difficult sampling is taken care of. The more useful Stan can be in a wider range of situations, the better.
>
> One of the reasons why one might move away from Stan to custom code is because the problem is "too hard" in some sense - perhaps the number of data points is too large and requires special techniques.  Perhaps there are linear algebra operations which scale as some poor function of the number of data points.  Gaussian Process methods are the best example of this, where naive implementations scale as O(N^3).
>
> Perhaps it is useful to start a wishlist of features which can help extend the usefulness of Stan in this way, by making it feasible to a wider range of problems.
>
> In the context of Gaussian Process regression, there are a number of ways of getting around the O(N^3) method, but one way is the use of a conjugate gradient approximation to find the approximate inverse of the covariance matrix.  Perhaps a Stan function which finds the approximate matrix inverse of a matrix C would be useful, eg approxinverse(matrix C, tolerance e), where e is the fractional tolerance.   If you are sampling the hyperparameters as well, you will need a way of getting the determinant of the covariance matrix fast as well, or the call to multi_normal will spend O(N^3) time calculating the determinant.
>
> Any other thoughts?
>
>
>

the random number generator a very big step (more than you'd
have time to genrate), thus making the draws in the different chains
come from different slices of the pseudo-random number sequence
determined by the seed.

This works the same way in the other interfaces, too.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.body_plain:
We're in the middle of writing a proposal for funding
to extend Stan to include, among other things, a number of
more scalable approaches, including:

  * data-parallel EP

  * data-streaming VB

  * maximum marginal likelihood (MML)

  * structured matrices (particularly banded and blocked)
    for GPs and other applications

  * sparse and ragged data structures

  * stiff ODE solving

We're very open to suggestions.

Keep in mind that for both our approach to sampling (HMC) and
optimization (L-BFGS), we need gradients of any operations we
employ.

Even without moving to Riemannian HMC, which introduces local
covariance matrix scaling issues, we wouldn't mind being able to
robustly esitmate a global covariance matrix for Euclidean HMC.
L-BFGS does this in its own way already.  And we'd very much like
to do that in a way that isn't O(n^3) for n x n covariance
matrices.

We've been encouraging people to use Cholesky-factor parameterizations
of covariance estimators as it cuts down on some of the algebra and
is more numerically stable.

- Bob

On Oct 15, 2014, at 6:17 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> Stan is very useful because of its flexibility as an MCMC langauge.  It is possible to get something working quickly and reasonably effectively because the user has to express intentions in a fairly high-level way, whilst all the difficult sampling is taken care of. The more useful Stan can be in a wider range of situations, the better.
>
> One of the reasons why one might move away from Stan to custom code is because the problem is "too hard" in some sense - perhaps the number of data points is too large and requires special techniques.  Perhaps there are linear algebra operations which scale as some poor function of the number of data points.  Gaussian Process methods are the best example of this, where naive implementations scale as O(N^3).
>
> Perhaps it is useful to start a wishlist of features which can help extend the usefulness of Stan in this way, by making it feasible to a wider range of problems.
>
> In the context of Gaussian Process regression, there are a number of ways of getting around the O(N^3) method, but one way is the use of a conjugate gradient approximation to find the approximate inverse of the covariance matrix.  Perhaps a Stan function which finds the approximate matrix inverse of a matrix C would be useful, eg approxinverse(matrix C, tolerance e), where e is the fractional tolerance.   If you are sampling the hyperparameters as well, you will need a way of getting the determinant of the covariance matrix fast as well, or the call to multi_normal will spend O(N^3) time calculating the determinant.
>
> Any other thoughts?
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan for large data sets and hard problems - approximations etc
messages.body_plain:
Bitter “old” man rant: there’s really no utility of having a discussion about
extending Stan without having actual goals in mind.  EP, VP, and MML
can be great data exploration tools but they will never admit robust
uncertainty modeling in complex systems, nor are they designed to.
Full Bayes will always be the most challenging goal but also provide
the biggest gains; adding new data structures (sparse or banded
matrices, etc) and functions (stiff ODEs) will help certain problems
but there are many such improvements and we’ll have to take
them one at a time as we see the motivation (developer help is
always welcome!).

Consequently I think making vague statements is not particularly
helpful.  If there are real models motivated by real problems that
don’t fit in Stan then let’s talk specifics.  Otherwise it’s just
un-actionable speculation.

For example, when does the N^{3} scaling of a GP really start mattering?
When N is large?  But when is N large?  Are you trying to fit a GP over
many dimensions? What happens to GPs that try to fit on many-dimensional
latent spaces?  Turns out lots of problems that can dwarf the N^{3}
complexity.

Stan has much room to grow — let’s do it right.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael.  Perhaps it would help in our proposal if we were to list specific examples of where we want these sorts of algorithms.  One example is pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic models with hundreds or thousands of patients.  These models can run slowly and it would be useful to have faster approximations.  Another example is hierarchical logistic regressions such as what we use to do multilevel regression and poststratification for survey data.  Again, full Bayes can be slow and people are running lmer (which has lots and lots of problems, most notably an extreme inflexibility when it comes to specifying priors or otherwise regularizing the inferences) as alternatives.  Another example are Gaussian process decomposition models such as we used in the birthday example on the cover of BDA3.  Again, this is a model we can write down but which we simply can’t fit in reasomable time in Stan.  It’s a little embarrassing for the example on the cover of my book to not be fittable!
I hope this helps (both for you and for the proposal)
See you
A

In Stan, real variables declared in transformed data, transformed parameters, and local variables are initialized to NaN, not a number. See http://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/NaN. messages.body_plain:
Three suggestions.

1.   You don't need to save yHat as a transformed parameter if you don't
     need it in the output.  You can make it a local variable in the model.
     Then you'd have to recompute it in the generated quantities block, but
     you can also do that as a local variable.  Then you don't output yHat.

2.   You don't want to try to set c[k] to cu[k] - cu[1].  That doesn't
     identify the cu because they can all shift and you get the same behavior.
     Instead, do something like declaring cu as pos_ordered[K-2], then setting
     c[1] to 0, and all c[k] to cu[k-1].

3.   You can use the non-centered parameterization for alpha.  Define
     alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1) and then define alpha <- muAlpha + sigma_alpha * alpha_raw.
     This is much faster when there's not much data to estimate alpha with.
     It may not matter here if alpha is well identified by the model.

- Bob

Dear Bob and other Stan Users,

I am looking at the WAIC example code for the simple regression example in BDA, p. 177

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/473

and I am working on applying it to my models, which are variants of reinforcement learning using a softmax function on the expected values to compute an action probability (= model prediction of data (subject choices)). This in turn is usually used to compute the log likelihood of the model.

>From the example code I gather that in order to compute WAIC I need to get a log likelihood for every data point. In my case, I have several subjects doing an experiment with about 64 - 200 trials depending on the task. Following the example, I think I should get log likelihood distribution for every data point in every subject, which get into the range of 5000 - 120000 posteriors of log likelihoods. Would this be the recommendation of the experts or should I rather calculate a likelihood per subject by summing/averaging over all trials in a participant?

Furthermore, the example code also uses colMeans to average over MCMC samples. Is this also a valid approach, if I have very skewed posteriors, or is this only valid for almost symmetric unimodal posteriors? (The histograms for log_lik in the simple regression example definitely look like symmetric and unimodal.)

Thanks a lot for your insights.
Jan

--
Jan Glaescher
glae...@gmail.com

messages.subject: Re: WAIC for multiple subjects
messages.subject_clean: WAIC for multiple subjects
messages.body_plain:
Hello, Jan.

Regarding the code, below is a slightly more robust version of the R code that Drs. Gelman and Vehtari used in their paper on WAIC, perhaps you may find it helpful. Just note that the Gelman & Vehtari code does not put loo-cv on the deviance scale. If you want to, just multiply it by -2.

WAIC <- function(stanfit){
  colVars <- function(M){
    vars <- M[1, ]
    for (n in seq_along(vars)) vars[n] <- var(M[, n])
    return(vars)
  }
  log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
  dim(log_lik) <- if (length(dim(log_lik)) == 1) c(length(log_lik), 1) else
    c(dim(log_lik)[1], prod(dim(log_lik)[2:length(dim(log_lik))]))
  S <- nrow(log_lik)
  n <- ncol(log_lik)
  lpd <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)))
  p_waic <- colVars(log_lik)
  elpd_waic <- lpd - p_waic
  waic <- -2 * elpd_waic
  loo_weights_raw <- 1 / exp(log_lik - max(log_lik))
  loo_weights_normalized <- loo_weights_raw/
    matrix(colMeans(loo_weights_raw), nrow=S, ncol=n, byrow=TRUE)
  loo_weights_regularized <- pmin(loo_weights_normalized, sqrt(S))
  elpd_loo <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik) * loo_weights_regularized) /
                  colMeans(loo_weights_regularized))
  p_loo <- lpd - elpd_loo
  pointwise <- cbind(waic, lpd, p_waic, elpd_waic, p_loo, elpd_loo)
  total <- colSums(pointwise)
  se <- sqrt(n * colVars(pointwise))
  return(list(waic=total["waic"], elpd_waic=total["elpd_waic"],
              p_waic=total["p_waic"], elpd_loo=total["elpd_loo"], p_loo=total["p_loo"],
              pointwise=pointwise, total=total, se=se))
}

As for the use of colMeans, all of the xAIC measures are based on an expectation--that of the log predictive density for the existing data. Much of the difference is in how these are adjusted for the inherent bias of testing against the training data. The benefit of WAIC vs. DIC {and yes, I'm probably breaking rigor here} is that the calculations are not done conditioned against the "plug in" Bayesian posterior of the parameters, but at the mean of the distributions of each of the points themselves, but it is still a penalized expectation measure, thus the need for for colMeans/colVars. If the distribution of the posterior of each data point is highly skewed, some of that should be captured in colVars. If you haven't seen it already, you'll probably find this helpful:<www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf>>

Hope that helps!

Avi

messages.subject: Re: WAIC for multiple subjects
messages.subject_clean: WAIC for multiple subjects
messages.body_plain:
You should first decide whether you are interested in the predictive performance for one new trial or for one new subject. For example, in brain research it is usually more interesting to estimate the model predictive performance for new subject, so that it is more justified to say that the model generalizes to other people than just the observed people.

WAIC is an approximation of leave-one-out cross-validation and works if removing one data point changes the posterior only a little. In this case I would assume that removing a single trial observation would change the posterior only a little and WAIC would work well.

If you are interested in leave-one-subject-out you could consider the likelihood per subject, but since it is the total likelihood contribution from that subject, you need to compute as much as in leave-one-trial-out. WAIC approximation for leave-one-subject-out can work if removing one subject changes the posterior only a little, but since you are removing more information it is more likely to have a bigger change, too. In that case, you would need to make the leave-one-subject-out cross-validation by using k-fold-cross-validation where in each fold you leave on subject out.

I don't have a figure showing how WAIC would probably behave in leave-one-subject-out case, but WAIC has a certain similarity to importance sampling cross-validation, and you may look Figure 11 in
 Aki Vehtari and Jouko Lampinen (2002). Bayesian model assessment and comparison using cross-validation predictive densities. Neural Computation, 14(10):2439-2468.
 http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/publications/VehtariLampinen_NC2002_preprint.pdf
In that specific case, leave-one-data point-out worked, but leave-one-group of data-out did not.

Aki

> Hello, Jan.
>
> Regarding the code, below is a slightly more robust version of the R code that Drs. Gelman and Vehtari used in their paper on WAIC, perhaps you may find it helpful. Just note that the Gelman & Vehtari code does not put loo-cv on the deviance scale. If you want to, just multiply it by -2.
>
> WAIC <- function(stanfit){
>   colVars <- function(M){
>     vars <- M[1, ]
>     for (n in seq_along(vars)) vars[n] <- var(M[, n])
>     return(vars)
>   }
>   log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
>   dim(log_lik) <- if (length(dim(log_lik)) == 1) c(length(log_lik), 1) else
>     c(dim(log_lik)[1], prod(dim(log_lik)[2:length(dim(log_lik))]))
>   S <- nrow(log_lik)
>   n <- ncol(log_lik)
>   lpd <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)))
>   p_waic <- colVars(log_lik)
>   elpd_waic <- lpd - p_waic
>   waic <- -2 * elpd_waic
>   loo_weights_raw <- 1 / exp(log_lik - max(log_lik))
>   loo_weights_normalized <- loo_weights_raw/
>     matrix(colMeans(loo_weights_raw), nrow=S, ncol=n, byrow=TRUE)
>   loo_weights_regularized <- pmin(loo_weights_normalized, sqrt(S))
>   elpd_loo <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik) * loo_weights_regularized) /
>                   colMeans(loo_weights_regularized))
>   p_loo <- lpd - elpd_loo
>   pointwise <- cbind(waic, lpd, p_waic, elpd_waic, p_loo, elpd_loo)
>   total <- colSums(pointwise)
>   se <- sqrt(n * colVars(pointwise))
>   return(list(waic=total["waic"], elpd_waic=total["elpd_waic"],
>               p_waic=total["p_waic"], elpd_loo=total["elpd_loo"], p_loo=total["p_loo"],
>               pointwise=pointwise, total=total, se=se))
> }
>
> As for the use of colMeans, all of the xAIC measures are based on an expectation--that of the log predictive density for the existing data. Much of the difference is in how these are adjusted for the inherent bias of testing against the training data. The benefit of WAIC vs. DIC {and yes, I'm probably breaking rigor here} is that the calculations are not done conditioned against the "plug in" Bayesian posterior of the parameters, but at the mean of the distributions of each of the points themselves, but it is still a penalized expectation measure, thus the need for for colMeans/colVars. If the distribution of the posterior of each data point is highly skewed, some of that should be captured in colVars. If you haven't seen it already, you'll probably find this helpful:<www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf>>
>
> Hope that helps!
>
> Avi

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jan.

What I forgot was that shorter code could not be applied to a stanfit item, but to the extracted matrix of log probabilities. As I'm not sure how your data is set up, it isn't directly applicable. However, realizing that the pointmatrix (or whatever the input was named) is a matrix where the columns are the data points and the rows are the observations of the densities at those point at each iteration of the simulation, you should be able to adjust the shorter code as needed. Otherwise, the longer code should be able to be applied to any stanfit item.

One other possible difference of which you should be aware, is that for the stan models I built, I capture the densities themselves. I beleive Gelman and Vetari capture log-densities. Looking at the code should identify which was used.

Thanks,

Avi

>
> What I forgot was that shorter code could not be applied to a stanfit item, but to the extracted matrix of log probabilities. As I'm not sure how your data is set up, it isn't directly applicable. However, realizing that the pointmatrix (or whatever the input was named) is a matrix where the columns are the data points and the rows are the observations of the densities at those point at each iteration of the simulation, you should be able to adjust the shorter code as needed. Otherwise, the longer code should be able to be applied to any stanfit item.
>
> One other possible difference of which you should be aware, is that for the stan models I built, I capture the densities themselves. I beleive Gelman and Vetari capture log-densities. Looking at the code should identify which was used.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Avi
>
> On Tuesday, October 21, 2014 2:19:24 PM UTC-4, glae...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Avi,
> >
> > thanks a lot for your answer and your code, both of which I find really helpful. In the email digest I have seen that you actually posted a much shorter R code, but in the web interface it is marked as deleted. Should I ignore this shorter code version then?
> >
> > Thanks a lot,
> > Jan
> >
> > On Monday, October 20, 2014 8:30:22 PM UTC+2, Avraham Adler wrote:
> > > Hello, Jan.
> > >
> > > Regarding the code, below is a slightly more robust version of the R code that Drs. Gelman and Vehtari used in their paper on WAIC, perhaps you may find it helpful. Just note that the Gelman & Vehtari code does not put loo-cv on the deviance scale. If you want to, just multiply it by -2.
> > >
> > > WAIC <- function(stanfit){
> > >   colVars <- function(M){
> > >     vars <- M[1, ]
> > >     for (n in seq_along(vars)) vars[n] <- var(M[, n])
> > >     return(vars)
> > >   }
> > >   log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
> > >   dim(log_lik) <- if (length(dim(log_lik)) == 1) c(length(log_lik), 1) else
> > >     c(dim(log_lik)[1], prod(dim(log_lik)[2:length(dim(log_lik))]))
> > >   S <- nrow(log_lik)
> > >   n <- ncol(log_lik)
> > >   lpd <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)))
> > >   p_waic <- colVars(log_lik)
> > >   elpd_waic <- lpd - p_waic
> > >   waic <- -2 * elpd_waic
> > >   loo_weights_raw <- 1 / exp(log_lik - max(log_lik))
> > >   loo_weights_normalized <- loo_weights_raw/
> > >     matrix(colMeans(loo_weights_raw), nrow=S, ncol=n, byrow=TRUE)
> > >   loo_weights_regularized <- pmin(loo_weights_normalized, sqrt(S))
> > >   elpd_loo <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik) * loo_weights_regularized) /
> > >                   colMeans(loo_weights_regularized))
> > >   p_loo <- lpd - elpd_loo
> > >   pointwise <- cbind(waic, lpd, p_waic, elpd_waic, p_loo, elpd_loo)
> > >   total <- colSums(pointwise)
> > >   se <- sqrt(n * colVars(pointwise))
> > >   return(list(waic=total["waic"], elpd_waic=total["elpd_waic"],
> > >               p_waic=total["p_waic"], elpd_loo=total["elpd_loo"], p_loo=total["p_loo"],
> > >               pointwise=pointwise, total=total, se=se))
> > > }
> > >
> > > As for the use of colMeans, all of the xAIC measures are based on an expectation--that of the log predictive density for the existing data. Much of the difference is in how these are adjusted for the inherent bias of testing against the training data. The benefit of WAIC vs. DIC {and yes, I'm probably breaking rigor here} is that the calculations are not done conditioned against the "plug in" Bayesian posterior of the parameters, but at the mean of the distributions of each of the points themselves, but it is still a penalized expectation measure, thus the need for for colMeans/colVars. If the distribution of the posterior of each data point is highly skewed, some of that should be captured in colVars. If you haven't seen it already, you'll probably find this helpful:<www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf>>
> > >
> > > Hope that helps!
> > >
> > > Avi
> > >
> > > On Monday, October 20, 2014 12:39:05 PM UTC-4, glae...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Dear Bob and other Stan Users,
> > > >
> > > > I am looking at the WAIC example code for the simple regression example in BDA, p. 177
> > > >
> > > > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/473
> > > >
> > > > and I am working on applying it to my models, which are variants of reinforcement learning using a softmax function on the expected values to compute an action probability (= model prediction of data (subject choices)). This in turn is usually used to compute the log likelihood of the model.
> > > >
> > > > From the example code I gather that in order to compute WAIC I need to get a log likelihood for every data point. In my case, I have several subjects doing an experiment with about 64 - 200 trials depending on the task. Following the example, I think I should get log likelihood distribution for every data point in every subject, which get into the range of 5000 - 120000 posteriors of log likelihoods. Would this be the recommendation of the experts or should I rather calculate a likelihood per subject by summing/averaging over all trials in a participant?
> > > >
> > > > Furthermore, the example code also uses colMeans to average over MCMC samples. Is this also a valid approach, if I have very skewed posteriors, or is this only valid for almost symmetric unimodal posteriors? (The histograms for log_lik in the simple regression example definitely look like symmetric and unimodal.)
> > > >
> > > > Thanks a lot for your insights.
> > > > Jan
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > --
> > > > Jan Glaescher
> > > > glae...@gmail.com
> > > >

> > x2 <- rnorm(100)

> > data {
> >    int<lower=0> N;

> >    vector[N] x2;
> >        real nu;
> > }
> > parameters {
> >    real beta_0;
> >    real beta_1;
> >    real beta_2;
> >       real<lower=0> sigma_e;
> >       vector[N] e;
> > }
> > model {
> >       e ~ student_t(nu, 0, sigma_e);
> >       sigma_e ~ cauchy(0, 1);
> >    y ~ binomial_logit(10, beta_0 + beta_1 * x1 + beta_2 * x2 + e);
> > }
> > '
> > # Run the model
> > fit <- stan(model_code = model1, data = df, iter = 4000, chains = 2)
> > print(fit)
> >

messages.subject: v2.5 released: Stan, RStan, PyStan, CmdStan, MatlabStan, Stan.jl
messages.subject_clean: v2.5 released: Stan, RStan, PyStan, CmdStan, MatlabStan, Stan.jl
messages.body_plain:
Stan 2.5 is official.

As usual, you can find everything from the home page:

  http://mc-stan.org

and you can drop us a line on the stan-users group if you have
problems with installs or questions about Stan or coding particular
models.

We'd like to welcome two new interfaces:

  * MatlabStan by Brian Lau

  * Stan.jl (for Julia) by Rob Goedman

The new interface home pages are linked from the Stan home page.

The release notes are appended below.

- Stan Dev Team

v2.5.0 (20 October 2014)
======================================================================

New Features
----------------------------------------
* ordinary differential equation solver, implemented by coupling
  the user-specified system with its sensitivities (#771)
* add reject() statement for user-defined rejections/exceptions (#458)
* new num_elements() functions that applies to all containers (#1026)
* added is_nan() and is_inf() functions (#592)
* nested reverse-mode autodiff, primarily for ode solver (#1031)
* added get_lp() function to remove any need for bare lp__  (#470)
* new functions cbind() and rbind() like those in R (#787)
* added modulus function in a way tht is consistent with integer
  division across platforms (#577)
* exposed pareto_type_2_rng (#580)
* added Frechet distribution and multi_gp_cholesky distribution
  (thanks to Alexey Stukalov for both)

Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* removed Eigen code insertion for numeric traits and replaced
  with order-independent metaprogram (#1065)
* cleaned up error messages to provide clearer error context
  and more informative messages (#640)
* extensive tests for higher order autodiff in densities (#823)
* added context factory
* deprecated lkj_cov density (#865)
* trying again with informational/rejection message (#223)
* more code moved from interfaces into Stan common libraries,
  including a var_context factory for configuration
* moved example models to own repo (stan-dev/example-models) and
  included as submodule for stan-dev/stan (#314)
* added per-iteration interrupt handler to BFGS optimizer (#768)
* worked around unused function warnings from gcc (#796)
* fixed error messages in vector to array conversion (#579, thanks
  Kevin S. Van Horn)
* fixed gp-fit.stan example to be as efficient as manual
  version (#782)
* update to Eigen version 3.2.2 (#1087)

Builds
----------------------------------------
* pull out testing into Python script for developers to simplify
  makes
* libstan dependencies handled properly and regenerate
  dependencies, including working around bug in GNU
  make 3.8.1 (#1058, #1061, #1062)

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------------
* deal with covariant return structure in functions (allows
  data-only variables to alternate with parameter version);  involved
  adding new traits metaprograms promote_scalar and
  promote_scalar_type (#849)
* fixed error message on check_nonzero_size (#1066)
* fix arg config printing after random seed generation (#1049)
* logical conjunction and disjunction operators short circuit (#593)
* clean up parser bug preventing variables starting with reserved
  names (#866)
* fma() function calls underlying platform fma (#667)
* remove upper bound on number of function arguments (#867)
* cleaned up code to remove compiler warnings (#1034)
* share likely() and unlikely() macros to avoid redundancy warnings (#1002)
* complete review of function library for NaN behavior and consistency
  of calls for double and autodiff values, with extensive
  documentation and extensive new unit tests for this and other,
  ehances NaN testing in built-in test functions (several dozen issues
  in the #800 to #902 range)
* fixing Eigen assert bugs with NO_DEBUG in tests (#904)
* fix to makefile to allow builds in g++ 4.4 (thanks to Ewan Dunbar)
* fix precedence of exponentiation in language (#835)
* allow size zero inputs in data and initialization (#683)

Documentation
----------------------------------------
* new chapter on differential equation solver
* new sections on default priors for regression coefficients and
  scales, including hierarchical and multivariate based on
  full Cholesky parameterization
* new part on algorithms, which chapters on HMC/NUTS, optimization,
  and diagnostics
* new chapter on models with latent discrete parameters
* using latexmk through make for LaTeX compilation
* changed page numbers to beg contiguous throughout so page numbers
  match PDF viewer page number
* all user-supplied corrections applied from next-manual issue
* section on identifiability with priors, including discussion of K-1
  parameterization of softmax and IRT
* new section on convergence monitoring
* extensive corrections from Andrew Gelman on regression models
  and notation
* added discussion of hurdle model in zero inflation section
* update built-in function doc to clarify several behaviors (#1025)

messages.body_plain:
The gradient looks fine.  The new Stan 2.5 manual has an explanation of
what's reported.  It's basically a comparison of the built-in autodiff
and finite differences on the unconstrained scale.

We don't really do Bayes factor calculations because Andrew prefers
model expansion, so I haven't had any experience doing this.

That product-space paper costs $36 until I get back inside
Columbia's network.  I found something similar in terms of authors
and content online on Michael Lee's site:

  http://www.socsci.uci.edu/~mdlee/LodewyckxEtAl2009.pdf

It looks like from figure 3 that the mixture is at the individual level,
but share a mixture parameter hat-pi (which confused me, because hats are
usually used for estimates, not naming parameters).

Do both models fit the data the way you'd expect without
the mixture?

Can you compute Bayes factors for other models using the same
technique?

I'm not very familiar with these calculations, but I'd watch out
for normalization issues --- the densities in Stan are not
normalized in the sampling formulation, only in the increment_log_prob
with the _log density functions.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If the model is a simple expression, the irrelevant parameters for a subset could be detected by making a fast dummy pass though the likelihood function and tainting the parameters as we go.

With if statements, recursion, etc, a real pass can be made without AD, followed by an AD pass that knows the support of the gradient.

After the parameters are updated (for a given batch), the support is unlikely to have changed, and it can be used as a guess for the next evaluation, refining it with more (or less) parameters if inadequate.

It gets murkier when working with matrices though.

I'm replying to on old thread, which may provide more context.

The idea is that some techniques allow one to sample by computing the likelihood function on random subsets of the data. For this to be efficient however, one needs to know how parameters relate to these subsets.

One approach is to explicitly index some parameters (typically some hidden variables) along with the observations. However, I was pointing out that such a relationship could be detected automatically.

messages.body_plain:
This is the same data slicing idea we need for
EP and VB.

We've been thinking along similar lines for
detecting Markov blankets of discrete parameters.

As long as we (1) pin down the conditionals in the language
to not touch parameters, and (2) don't do conditionals inside
our autodiff function implementations, we get a static expression
tree.

It's very tempting to start thinking about code-generating
autodiff at that point.

But what we'll probably do is somehow link the parameters to
the data in the language.  Haven't figured out how we'll annotate
that in the log density function though.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extracting warm up samples
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extracting warm up samples
messages.body_plain:
There's an inc_warmup flag and also a permuted flag.
The default for the former is false and the latter is true.
There's no point in including warmup and permuting, so make
sure to set permute=FALSE when setting inc_warmup=TRUE.

By default, traceplot will include the warmup samples.

But you can't use them for inference, which is why they're
not returned by default by extract.

- Bob

> v2.5.0 (20 October 2014)
> ======================================================================
>
> New Features
> ----------------------------------------
> * ordinary differential equation solver, implemented by coupling
>   the user-specified system with its sensitivities (#771)
> * add reject() statement for user-defined rejections/exceptions (#458)
> * new num_elements() functions that applies to all containers (#1026)
> * added is_nan() and is_inf() functions (#592)

> * added Frechet distribution and multi_gp_cholesky distribution
>   (thanks to Alexey Stukalov for both)
>
> Enhancements
> ----------------------------------------
> * removed Eigen code insertion for numeric traits and replaced
>   with order-independent metaprogram (#1065)
> * cleaned up error messages to provide clearer error context
>   and more informative messages (#640)
> * extensive tests for higher order autodiff in densities (#823)
> * added context factory
> * deprecated lkj_cov density (#865)
> * trying again with informational/rejection message (#223)
> * more code moved from interfaces into Stan common libraries,
>   including a var_context factory for configuration
> * moved example models to own repo (stan-dev/example-models) and
>   included as submodule for stan-dev/stan (#314)
> * added per-iteration interrupt handler to BFGS optimizer (#768)
> * worked around unused function warnings from gcc (#796)
> * fixed error messages in vector to array conversion (#579, thanks
>   Kevin S. Van Horn)
> * fixed gp-fit.stan example to be as efficient as manual
>   version (#782)
> * update to Eigen version 3.2.2 (#1087)
>
> Builds
> ----------------------------------------
> * pull out testing into Python script for developers to simplify
>   makes
> * libstan dependencies handled properly and regenerate
>   dependencies, including working around bug in GNU
>   make 3.8.1 (#1058, #1061, #1062)
>
> Bug Fixes
> ----------------------------------------
> * deal with covariant return structure in functions (allows
>   data-only variables to alternate with parameter version);  involved
>   adding new traits metaprograms promote_scalar and
>   promote_scalar_type (#849)
> * fixed error message on check_nonzero_size (#1066)
> * fix arg config printing after random seed generation (#1049)
> * logical conjunction and disjunction operators short circuit (#593)
> * clean up parser bug preventing variables starting with reserved
>   names (#866)
> * fma() function calls underlying platform fma (#667)
> * remove upper bound on number of function arguments (#867)
> * cleaned up code to remove compiler warnings (#1034)
> * share likely() and unlikely() macros to avoid redundancy warnings (#1002)
> * complete review of function library for NaN behavior and consistency
>   of calls for double and autodiff values, with extensive
>   documentation and extensive new unit tests for this and other,
>   ehances NaN testing in built-in test functions (several dozen issues
>   in the #800 to #902 range)

> * new part on algorithms, which chapters on HMC/NUTS, optimization,

On Oct 23, 2014, at 12:09 PM, Sean O'Riordain <seor...@tcd.ie> wrote:

> I'm not sure how you might put this on the "RStan Getting Started" page - but not everybody has as much as 6gb so that might be a common enough cause of install failure...

I'm not sure how it varies by platform, either, but you're right,
we should have memory requirements on the install page.

It's hard to remember that not everyone has 8 GB.  I've been running on
computers with at least 8GB for over a decade!  One book I love had some
advice I hate:  give developers the slowest computers rather than the
fastest ones.

I would strongly recommend that anyone who can afford it upgrade their
memory to at least 8GB if not 16GB.

> As a nice to have feature... it'd be nice to have a faster compile of a model - currently on this not too slow Dell XPS-laptop it takes about 28 seconds to compile a model... which is a bit tedious when experimenting with models and importantly it is not enough time to make a coffee! :-)

I take it getting a faster computer and coffee maker is out
of the question.

How are you compiling?  On my three-year old Macbook Pro (quad-core 2.3GHz i7 CPU,
16GB 1600MHz DDR3 memory), compile times at -O3 are closer to 10 seconds with clang++.
I'm guessing you must be using g++ or some other compiler than clang++.

It is possible to compile models with less optimization.  They will
take an order of magnitude (or more) more time to run at -O0 than at -O3,
but this may be a win for a model that takes less than a second to fit.
And they'll compile much faster at -O0.

We're unlikely to drastically speed up compile time.  The
rock and hard place we're caught between are too many instantiations
of our templated function to sensibly precompile (e.g.., 10s of thousands
just for Studnent-t) and the slowness of compiling templated functions.
Not to mention lack of good C++ tools on Windows.

- Bob

> > - Stan Dev Team

> > v2.5.0 (20 October 2014)
> > ======================================================================
> >
> > New Features
> > ----------------------------------------
> > * ordinary differential equation solver, implemented by coupling
> >   the user-specified system with its sensitivities (#771)

> > ----------------------------------------
> > * removed Eigen code insertion for numeric traits and replaced
> >   with order-independent metaprogram (#1065)
> > * cleaned up error messages to provide clearer error context
> >   and more informative messages (#640)
> > * extensive tests for higher order autodiff in densities (#823)
> > * added context factory
> > * deprecated lkj_cov density (#865)
> > * trying again with informational/rejection message (#223)
> > * more code moved from interfaces into Stan common libraries,
> >   including a var_context factory for configuration
> > * moved example models to own repo (stan-dev/example-models) and
> >   included as submodule for stan-dev/stan (#314)
> > * added per-iteration interrupt handler to BFGS optimizer (#768)
> > * worked around unused function warnings from gcc (#796)

> >   Kevin S. Van Horn)

> >   version (#782)

> > * pull out testing into Python script for developers to simplify
> >   makes

> >   dependencies, including working around bug in GNU
> >   make 3.8.1 (#1058, #1061, #1062)
> >

> > ----------------------------------------
> > * deal with covariant return structure in functions (allows
> >   data-only variables to alternate with parameter version);  involved
> >   adding new traits metaprograms promote_scalar and
> >   promote_scalar_type (#849)
> > * fixed error message on check_nonzero_size (#1066)
> > * fix arg config printing after random seed generation (#1049)
> > * logical conjunction and disjunction operators short circuit (#593)
> > * clean up parser bug preventing variables starting with reserved
> >   names (#866)
> > * fma() function calls underlying platform fma (#667)
> > * remove upper bound on number of function arguments (#867)
> > * cleaned up code to remove compiler warnings (#1034)
> > * share likely() and unlikely() macros to avoid redundancy warnings
> > (#1002)
> > * complete review of function library for NaN behavior and consistency
> >   of calls for double and autodiff values, with extensive
> >   documentation and extensive new unit tests for this and other,
> >   ehances NaN testing in built-in test functions (several dozen issues
> >   in the #800 to #902 range)
> > * fixing Eigen assert bugs with NO_DEBUG in tests (#904)
> > * fix to makefile to allow builds in g++ 4.4 (thanks to Ewan Dunbar)
> > * fix precedence of exponentiation in language (#835)
> > * allow size zero inputs in data and initialization (#683)
> >
> > Documentation
> > ----------------------------------------
> > * new chapter on differential equation solver
> > * new sections on default priors for regression coefficients and
> >   scales, including hierarchical and multivariate based on
> >   full Cholesky parameterization
> > * new part on algorithms, which chapters on HMC/NUTS, optimization,
> >   and diagnostics
> > * new chapter on models with latent discrete parameters
> > * using latexmk through make for LaTeX compilation

> > * all user-supplied corrections applied from next-manual issue

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,
Well 30 seconds is not really long enough to make a *good* coffee... :-)

While the "desktop" machines I use have 16-128 Gb of memory, this three year old Dell XPS laptop - "high performance" for its' day - all we could afford under the budget... well the CPU is...
Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-2630QM CPU @ 2.00GHz (fam: 06, model: 2a, stepping: 07)
It came with 6Gb memory and it can take at most 8Gb.
Running on Ubuntu Linux, I've deliberately run things at the defaults... I've not installed clang... so g++ it is...

Similarly I haven't changed the defaults for optimization in Stan... I might look into trying that...

I seem to recollect that it that Bill Gates insisted that his developers used modest machines... but that was about 1996 ? maybe?

As an aside, I noticed that the log-likelihood for my model has sufficient statistics that can be pre-calculated in the transformed data block which *dramatically* speeds up the time per iteration... since looping is no longer required :-)

Sean

error: Command "gcc -fno-strict-aliasing -I/Users/noahsilbert/anaconda/include -arch x86_64 -DNDEBUG -g -fwrapv -O3 -Wall -Wstrict-prototypes -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS -Ipystan/stan/src -Ipystan/stan/lib/eigen_3.2.0 -Ipystan/stan/lib/boost_1.54.0 -c pystan/stan/src/stan/agrad/rev/var_stack.cpp -o build/temp.macosx-10.5-x86_64-2.7/pystan/stan/src/stan/agrad/rev/var_stack.o" failed with exit status 69

I am at a loss to understand what this means or what I can do to get pystan to work on this computer. Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

> > > - Stan Dev Team
> > >
> > >
> > > v2.5.0 (20 October 2014)
> > > ======================================================================
> > >
> > > New Features
> > > ----------------------------------------
> > > * ordinary differential equation solver, implemented by coupling
> > >   the user-specified system with its sensitivities (#771)

> > >
> > > Enhancements
> > > ----------------------------------------
> > > * removed Eigen code insertion for numeric traits and replaced
> > >   with order-independent metaprogram (#1065)
> > > * cleaned up error messages to provide clearer error context
> > >   and more informative messages (#640)
> > > * extensive tests for higher order autodiff in densities (#823)
> > > * added context factory
> > > * deprecated lkj_cov density (#865)
> > > * trying again with informational/rejection message (#223)
> > > * more code moved from interfaces into Stan common libraries,
> > >   including a var_context factory for configuration

> > > * added per-iteration interrupt handler to BFGS optimizer (#768)

> > > * fixed error messages in vector to array conversion (#579, thanks
> > >   Kevin S. Van Horn)
> > > * fixed gp-fit.stan example to be as efficient as manual
> > >   version (#782)
> > > * update to Eigen version 3.2.2 (#1087)
> > >
> > > Builds
> > > ----------------------------------------
> > > * pull out testing into Python script for developers to simplify
> > >   makes
> > > * libstan dependencies handled properly and regenerate
> > >   dependencies, including working around bug in GNU
> > >   make 3.8.1 (#1058, #1061, #1062)
> > >
> > > Bug Fixes
> > > ----------------------------------------
> > > * deal with covariant return structure in functions (allows
> > >   data-only variables to alternate with parameter version);  involved
> > >   adding new traits metaprograms promote_scalar and
> > >   promote_scalar_type (#849)
> > > * fixed error message on check_nonzero_size (#1066)
> > > * fix arg config printing after random seed generation (#1049)
> > > * logical conjunction and disjunction operators short circuit (#593)
> > > * clean up parser bug preventing variables starting with reserved
> > >   names (#866)
> > > * fma() function calls underlying platform fma (#667)
> > > * remove upper bound on number of function arguments (#867)
> > > * cleaned up code to remove compiler warnings (#1034)
> > > * share likely() and unlikely() macros to avoid redundancy warnings
> > > (#1002)
> > > * complete review of function library for NaN behavior and consistency
> > >   of calls for double and autodiff values, with extensive
> > >   documentation and extensive new unit tests for this and other,
> > >   ehances NaN testing in built-in test functions (several dozen issues
> > >   in the #800 to #902 range)
> > > * fixing Eigen assert bugs with NO_DEBUG in tests (#904)
> > > * fix to makefile to allow builds in g++ 4.4 (thanks to Ewan Dunbar)
> > > * fix precedence of exponentiation in language (#835)
> > > * allow size zero inputs in data and initialization (#683)
> > >
> > > Documentation
> > > ----------------------------------------
> > > * new chapter on differential equation solver
> > > * new sections on default priors for regression coefficients and
> > >   scales, including hierarchical and multivariate based on
> > >   full Cholesky parameterization
> > > * new part on algorithms, which chapters on HMC/NUTS, optimization,
> > >   and diagnostics
> > > * new chapter on models with latent discrete parameters
> > > * using latexmk through make for LaTeX compilation
> > > * changed page numbers to beg contiguous throughout so page numbers
> > >   match PDF viewer page number
> > > * all user-supplied corrections applied from next-manual issue
> > > * section on identifiability with priors, including discussion of K-1
> > >   parameterization of softmax and IRT
> > > * new section on convergence monitoring
> > > * extensive corrections from Andrew Gelman on regression models
> > >   and notation
> > > * added discussion of hurdle model in zero inflation section
> > > * update built-in function doc to clarify several behaviors (#1025)
> > >
> > >
> > >

messages.body_plain:
I am an R user and use Stan via rstan, but I prefer append_col and
append_row in Stan.

IMO many function names in R are accidental and occasionally not well
chosen (in particular, I very much resent the allocation c and t as
function names, which makes their use as single-letter local variables
bad style, if not exactly invalid). Also, while I am an "R user", I am a
C user, Julia user, and Lisp user too. So I don't see why Stan should
make an effort to follow any traditions of R when they are not the
optimal choice per se.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Figure 11.1 (pg. 99) in the manual for v2.5 gives the code for a change point model where at time s the Poisson rate parameter changes from the "early rate" e to the "late rate" l . I’m wondering what the best way is to code an extension of this model to allow for multiple change points. For example, suppose that there is also a rate for a middle period m, which would entail two change points s1 and s2 separating the three periods e, m and l. I can't figure out a good way to expand the code given on pg. 99 to appropriately marginalize out both of the change points. Thanks in advance for any advice.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Expanding change point model in section 11.2 of the manual
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Expanding change point model in section 11.2 of the manual
messages.body_plain:
Where you have the single loop in s for the changepoint, you
need to instead keep pairs.  Easiest way to do it would be
in a matrix:

  matrix[T,T] lp;
  lp <- rep_matrix(log_unif,T);
  for (s1 in 1:T)
    for (s2 in 1:T)
      for (t in 1:T)
        lp[s1,s2] <- lp[s1,s2]
                     + poisson_log(D[t], if_else(t < s1,
                                                 e, if_else(t < s2, m, l)));

and then in the model needs to be changed to convert the
matrix lp to a vector so it can be passed to log_sum_exp:

  increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(to_vector(lp)));

The problem is that as there are more change points, the
computational complexity grows.  You can see it intuitively
from the loops.

Suppose there are N items.  With a single change point, you
need to consider all N positions.  Each position requires
an amount N of work, so overall complexity is O(N^2).

With two change points you need to consider all (N choose 2)
change points.  That's a quadratic number of pairs, each
requiring an amount N of work, so overall complexity is O(N^3).

- Bob

P.S.  I'll add the discussion to the next manual.  This is a case
      where something like Metropolis or Gibbs has a big computational
      advantage in terms of iteration time, but this method should produce
      better mixing and also let you estimate all the tails that would never
      be visited by Gibbs or Metropolis.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] preventing underflow in a mixture model
messages.body_plain:
On Oct 23, 2014, at 7:56 PM, Martin Šmíra <smira....@gmail.com> wrote:

> The Bayes Factor is not really important here. Only thing where the model differs from the original one is the possibility of sampling from categorical_logit with two different parameters. First is givven by Delta learning rule and another by Decay leraning rule:
>
> // Delta Learning Rule
> Ev_delta[choice[s,t]] <- (1 - a_ind[s]) * Ev_delta[choice[s,t]] + a_ind[s] * v;
> // Decay Lerning Rule
> Ev_decay <- Ev_decay * a_ind[s];
> Ev_decay[choice[s,t]] <- Ev_decay[choice[s,t]] + v;
>
> choice[s,t+1] ~ categorical_logit(Ev_delta * theta);
>  {{OR (as a mixture)}}
> choice[s,t+1] ~ categorical_logit(Ev_decay * theta);

I'm confused by pretty much all of this. If you want
to code a mixture, you want to use

   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp1, lp2));

where lp1 and lp2 are the log probs of the two components being mixed,
including the mixing proportions.  For example, a mixture that I'd write
in math as:

  p(y) = lambda * normal(y|mu1,sigma1) + (1 - lambda) * normal(y|mu2,sigma2)

is coded as:

   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(lambda) + normal_log(y,mu1,sigma1),
                                  log1m(lambda) + normal_log(y,mu2,sigma2)));

First, it looks like a_ind[s] is some kind of mixing proportion.  But
it looks like you're mixing some kind of scalar multiplier?  I don't see
why the mixture defining Ev_delta is done on the logit scale.  But maybe a_ind
isn't a mixing proportion?

And then there's a move from t to t+1 that I don't get.

Why would you be multiplying by theta in both categorical logits?  What
is the type of theta and why is it the same in both cases?  And where does
it make sense to multiply on the logit scale?  That has the effect of
flattening or attenuating the probabilities depending on whether the
multipler is below or above zero.

If you could write down in ordinary math notation what the distribution
is supposed to be for choice[s,t] (I also don't get the t vs. t+1 above),
then it should be easy to code in Stan.

> If this would mix properly, then I can easily get the BF from the posterior mixing proportion.
>
> Q;  Do both models fit the data the way you'd expect without
> the mixture?
>   - Yes, I did, but I better check it again.
>
> Q:  Can you compute Bayes factors for other models using the same technique?
>    - Yes, I've already used this method, actually on a similar (PVL-Delta) model. This model was comparing two groups of subjects whether they come from the same hierarchical group distribution. And it worked like a charm, actually just in Stan, Jags version performed miserably (poor mixing). Actually I've heard that Jags (BUGS also I guess) in general has problem with this method. I guess that this approach is computationally demanding. Especially in this case where probabilities of each mixture part is on such a small scale.

If you have the A/B models in Stan and JAGS, could you send them along?
We're looking to write some papers on comparisons and looking for examples
that behave differently in Gibbs vs. HMC/NUTS.

> What do you mean by the normalization issues? I use "~" sampling statements only in 8 cases and they all are just normal(0, 1).

Categorical logit is what's being mixed, and it will always be normalized,
so that's not an issue.

> I thought that the paper is freely available, can you access it here (below)?
> https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Lodewyckx2011ATOBF.pdf

The link is to an illegally pirated copy that someone's hosting
on a web page.  As much as I hate closed-source journals, I'm not
advocating stealing.  The journal does let you buy open access for your
paper (their site says fees range from US$500 to US$5000:

  http://www.elsevier.com/about/open-access/open-access-journals

but only two authors seem to have taken them up on it in the last six
years:

  http://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-mathematical-psychology/open-access-articles/

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Oops -- didn't see Herra's comments before responding.

Yes, it does matter.   You need to split the parameters.
You can share the data.   Both sub-models are evaluated at each step
and then mixed.

The density that you are then defining is:

    p(lambda, theta1, theta2, y)

    = lambda * M1(theta1, y) + (1 - lambda) * M2(theta2, y)

or on the log scale:

   log p(lambda, theta1, theta2, y)

   = log_sum_exp(log(lambda)   + log M1(theta1, y),
                 log1m(lambda) + log M2(theta2, y))

where theta1 and theta2 are disjoint parameters and y is data,
which does not have to be duplicated.

I just wanted to make sure this was the density you intended
to estimate.  If so, if you split the parameters and estimate
lambda (what you called mix), then you should be good to go.

- Bob

messages.subject: Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

Firstly, I can't imagine this hasn't come up before (although I couldn't find anything via search); advance apologies for any duplication!

I'm about to spend a daunting amount of time writing test procedures for various Stan models in R (which I should have done some time ago), using standardish 'test set', 'training set' methods.

What makes the process laborious (and easy to goof up!) is repeatedly re-writing code to mirror Stan model specifications in R, to generate (MC) predicted values for a new dataset (a la Gelman and Hill). The method outlined under 'Predictions as Generated Quantities' in the manual (p. 58) looks good, but is a little restrictive in that predictive MC simulations can only be run during a fit (as far as I've understood).

The predict.xxx (and Andrew's 'sim') functions in R make this a breeze, for the packages where they're available.

I can immediately think of lots of reasons why doing something similar for Stan would be tricky! But is it possible?

I get the impression it would best be done on the C++ side (flipping lp incrementing functions to rng counterparts), but could an R programmer (me) contribute anything useful?

Brendan

messages.body_plain:
Yes, it's come up, but this group's pretty much impossible
to search.

This is not meant to be an excuse for not having a built-in capability, but
one advantage of having to duplicate the effort outside Stan is that the testing
is more robust.  If there's a mistake in the model, then just using
the broken model to generate test cases may not diagnose a problem.
It becomes a burden when you have to start lining up negative binomial
parameterizations --- bug again perhaps even more worth it for robustness.

To simulate in Stan, you need to take the model you built to
estimate, then rearrange declarations between data and parameters.
This will only work for continuous quantities.  Alternatively you
can use the rng blocks as you suggest, but in that case, you have to
rewrite the code, as well.  We can't just literally follow
the graphical model because there's never a graphical model declared
in Stan.

- Bob
