messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Warning messages
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Warning messages
messages.body_plain:
Technically, you want to worry when your chains don't mix well.
Diagnosing non-mixing is another matter.  One test that can be
done within Stan is to run with higher acceptance rate targets (delta
parameter), which will force smaller step sizes and increased numerical
stability, and make sure you get the same answer.  Just be warned that
smaller step sizes are proportionally slower in NUTS.

You can also start warmup with smaller step sizes, which may eliminate
these messages.

Informally, if the problem goes away during warmup and only occurs
occasionally (or infrequently, or pick your own temporal adverb that
means not very often) during sampling.  We don't have precise numbers for
this, but I'd be worried if you had the warning more than once every few
dozen iterations during sampling.

For efficiency and arithmetic stability, you almost never want to
use a covariance matrix variable.  See the new section in the manual
chapter on regression for a fully Cholesky factored approach that is
both faster and more arithmetically stable than using covariance matrix
parameters.

- Bob

P.S.  Temporal adverbs were a large part of my Ph.D. thesis
on the semantics intensional adverbs :-)  I'm told there's a special
hell for semanticists (and probably for theory manglers --- I mashed
up Davidsonian event semantics and Montagovian intensionality).

messages.body_plain:
You only need something centered roughly where you know the answer
will be and not excluding reasonable values.  And then maybe make it
a bit wider.  The point is that if you're expecting values in the -2 to 2
range, you want to convey that in the prior rather than having a prior
that's uniform, say from -1000 to 1000.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for helpful suggestions!

My data consists of responses (y) and two grouping variables (pp & rr), by being nested I meant that (in smaller scale) it would look like this:

pp rr
A  A
A  B
B  A
B  B
...

so each pp is a member of some rr groups, and each rr is a member of some pp groups, but they are randomly allocated and not each pp in in each rr group, and vice versa. And y is scaled so that it has mean = 0 and sd = 1, so modelling and interpretability becomes easier.

I changed my model a bit: added hierarchical priors, removed gamma priors etc. and it works better and gives exactly the same results as computed by lme4 package for R. I also found that sigma_rr had sd = 0, so I changed it to global sigma, and it's value also happens to be the same as computed by lme4. Lack of variability of this parameter could suggest that there's no point in estimating grouped sigma's, but it seems strange for me that there's no variability and no between-groups differences. Do I have to worry if sigma's sd is zero? What could I do about it?

Greetings,
Tim

> >   int<lower=0> R;
> >   int<lower=1> pp[N];
> >   int<lower=1> rr[N];
> >   real y[N];
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=0, upper=3> sigma_rr[R];
> >   real<lower=-6, upper=6> b_pp[P];
> >   real<lower=-6, upper=6> b_pp[R];
> > }
> > model {
> >   b_pp ~ normal(0, 1);
> >   b_rr ~ normal(0, 1);
> >   sigma_rr ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> >
> >   for (i in 1:N) {
> >     y[i] ~ normal(b_pp[pp[i]] + b_rr[rr[i]], sigma_rr[rr[i]]);
> >   }
> > }
>
> When you get a "straight" line is it literally constant?
> In that case, R-hat would be NaN.  What may be happening is
> that your parameters may be getting pinned (sigma_rr at 0 or
> 3, the coefficients at -6 or 6.).
>
> I'd try to start simpler and build up to this model.
> For instance, only use b_pp and use a single sigma rather
> than one varying by rr[i].  That should give you a feeling for
> the scales of b_pp and sigma_rr.
>
> You might also want to pull out an overall intercept if the
> data y isn't centered --- otherwise you're forcing b_pp or
> b_rr to pick up the slack even though they have centered priors.
>
> Eventually, I'd think you'd want a hierarchical prior for b_pp
> and b_rr.
>
> Also --- you may want to use different priors.  We don't recommend
> constraints to intervals nor do we recommend the super-diffuse
> gamma(0.001,0.001) priors on scale parameters --- there are three new sections in
> the 2.5 manual with a discussion of the priors we do recommend in the
> chapter on regression.
>
> - Bob

should probably not be using Cauchy(0,5) and the like for

You can use a gamma (not inverse gamma) on the scale and get
zero-avoiding behavior that doesn't pollute the estimates too much
Again, see the manual chapter and reference paper by Andrew and crew on zero-avoiding priors.

scale?  Or do you just mean it runs to below -800 or so on the log
scale and thus exp(-800) underflows to 0?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] mixed-effects model in stan
messages.body_plain:
What is nlme and are you sure you're fitting the same model?

With this kind of model, your problem is most likely identifiability.
You can often diagnose this empirically by plotting correlations of
parameters.

I think your problem may be here:

	// priors
	for (i in 1 : 4)
		beta [i] ~ normal (beta0 [i], 0.1 * beta0 [i]);

This isn't identified in itself because beta and beta0 are variables
and you only have a single observation.  But then I see
that you're using beta elsewhere, but it could still be a problem.

There are a lot of things you can do for efficiency
and numerical stability, too.

Most importantly, use a Cholesky-based parameterization
for Omega rather than decomposing it.  There's an extended
example in the priors section of the regression chapter in
the Stan 2.5 manual.

Then use a non-centered parameterization for hierarchical
priors --- there's also a discussion in the manual in the
chapter on reparameterizations.

You can pass vectors directly to increment_log_prob now,
so you don't need the sum() in sum(log_lik).

We have quad forms with diagonals, so you don't need to
create diagonal matrices and multiply.

You can replace

	for (i in 1 : 4) mu_prior [i] <- 0;

with

  mu_prior <- rep_vector(0.0, 4);

not that it's an issue in your code being in the transformed
data block.

Use local variables in the transformed parameters block so
things don't get saved, like D, L and DL (though you really want
to completely replace those using the direct Cholesky parameterization).

- Bob

people might understand already, but I still don't get it.  I'm confused

real example?

For instance, might A and B pick out media genres (e.g.,
action and romance), and the pp and rr denote preferences
for people in films and books?

> I changed my model a bit: added hierarchical priors, removed gamma priors etc. and it works better and gives exactly the same results as computed by lme4 package for R.

You won't always get the same result using MCMC and max marginal likelihood (MML),
because posterior modes and posterior means don't always coincide.

> I also found that sigma_rr had sd = 0, so I changed it to global sigma, and it's value also happens to be the same as computed by lme4. Lack of variability of this parameter could suggest that there's no point in estimating grouped sigma's, but it seems strange for me that there's no variability and no between-groups differences. Do I have to worry if sigma's sd is zero? What could I do about it?

I'd suggest reading Andrew and crew's papers on hierarchical
variance priors.  You can impose a prior that bounds estimates
away from 0, but you usually don't want to do that.  There can be a problem
in posteriors that probabability density is highest at zero variance
and all lower-level parameters being the same.

- Bob

Priors such as the lognormal cut off at 0 and are appropriate if you think the parameter can’t be very close to 0.  Priors such as the half-normal go all the way to 0 and are appropriate if you don’t want to rule out values very close to 0.
In general I don’t see any good reason to put a model on the inverse of a scale parameter.

messages.body_plain:
Using

  real<lower=0> x;

implicitly works on the log(x) scale and then applies exp() to
get back to positive.  That is, Stan treats x_raw as (-inf,inf) and
defines x <- exp(x_raw).  This also applies a Jacobian, allowing
you to define a sampling distribution for x, e.g.,

  x ~ lognormal(0,5);

If you explicitly define:

  real x;

with sampling distribution

  x ~ normal(1,5);

the computation is a bit different because we don't need to
apply the Jacobian to and from the lognormal.  So maybe it's more
arithmetically stable.

- Bob

Hello:

messages.body_plain:
If it is a generated quantity only, then you can declare it as a plain square matrix

matrix[4,4] Sigma;

that way, it won't do a positive definiteness check. Some of your realizations may be nearly singular but that is probably manageable.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] error when calculating covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
Sigma was not positive definite in the iteration where the error
arose.

It's hard to diagnose problems without the rest of the model, but
this is only going to work if sigma_u has only finite positive values
and L_Omega is the Cholesky factor for a covariance matrix (basically,
that just means finite values with positive diagonal).

Given that it's a generated quantity, if you declare Sigma as a matrix[4,4]
rather than as a cov_matrix[4], that test will be suppressed.

You can also print the whole matrix, which will happen before the
test (the tests for constraint violations occur at the end of blocks),
so you can see what's going on.

- Bob

P.S.  Sorry the current message is so confusing.  We're working on trying
      to clean this up for the next minor release (Stan 2.6).

messages.subject: Fitting a simple GP -- Cholesky issue?
messages.subject_clean: Fitting a simple GP -- Cholesky issue?
messages.body_plain:
Hi list. Louis and I are working on a GP model with Andrew for survey
responses and we came across something unexpected, wanted to see if
anyone knew what was going on, whether Stan was suppressing a relevant
error message or something else. Attached is a minimal working example
of a GP with Binomial observation model.

We're just using a dot product covariance function (k(x,x') = <x,x'> +
c) for the GP prior. We were expecting that this prior would give us
straight lines, as in my Shiny demo here (since it has a closed form
solution, I coded this up with a normal observation model, but for the
posterior mean it's pretty much equivalent):
https://flaxter.shinyapps.io/linearkernel/

Due to numerical issues (I think) it's not working in Stan, which you
can see if you run the code attached. Plot here:
https://www.dropbox.com/s/48l0n7021g5tv16/plot1.png?dl=0

All it takes to fix it is to add some noise to the main diagonal. Plot
here: https://www.dropbox.com/s/hpcnfqew1o303si/plot2.png?dl=0

No big deal now that I realize it, I'm just wondering what Stan did
when it took the cholesky decomposition, whether it was silently
having issues or what? Switching to y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma) gives
me the following when there's no extra noise on the main diagonal:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be
rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::multi_normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): LDLT_Factor of
covariance parameterunderlying matrix is not positive definite.
LDLT_Factor of covariance parameterlast conditional variance is
-3.46945e-018:0.
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained
variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either
severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Thoughts?
Seth

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Left-Censored data with differing censoring points per group.
messages.body_plain:
The truncated distributions are not vectorized.  But you could
do something like:

  for (n in 1:N_cs)
    y_cs ~ normal(mu_cs, y_sigma) T[0,U];

You've already declared y_cs with the appropriate constraint, which
is the critical part:

  real<lower=0, upper=U> y_cs[N_cs]; // estimates for censored response

So note that you are also truncating below at L=0, so that also needs
to be rolled in.

I don't think there's an easy way to vectorize all of this and still
get the lower and upper truncations right.  That's why we didn't build
it in.  If you unfold the density, what you have is this:

  Normal(z | mu, sigma) T[L,U]

  =def=              Normal(z | mu,sigma)
         ---------------------------------------------
         NormalCDF(U | mu,sigma) - NormalCDF(0 | mu,sigma)

and the problem with putting this on the log scale is that the
difference of CDFS is on the linear scale, whereas the result needs
to be on the log scale.  You can do it yourself and perhaps save a bit
of efficiency, but I think it'd be a lot easier to understand just
written using the truncation.

- Bob

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Fitting a simple GP -- Cholesky issue?
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, October 31, 2014 2:59:49 PM UTC-4, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> No big deal now that I realize it, I'm just wondering what Stan did
> when it took the cholesky decomposition, whether it was silently
> having issues or what? Switching to y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma) gives
> me the following when there's no extra noise on the main diagonal:

The multi_normal_choleksy() function trusts that L is a valid Cholesky factor, whereas multi_normal() checks that the covariance matrix is positive definite, which is numerically unstable. So, the former is better to use when you know that the covariance matrix is positive definite by construction.

Ben
